for-all-moonkind.story:
For All Moonkind is a volunteer nonprofit, founded in 2017 by Tim and Michelle Hanlon, that works to protect the places on the Moon where people and machines have landed. Michelle Hanlon is a professor of air and space law at the University of Mississippi. The name plays on a phrase used twice in the Apollo programme. The plaque Apollo 11 left on the Moon spoke of peace for all mankind, and Gene Cernan used the same words as Apollo 17 left.

The worry behind the group is simple. Many countries and companies plan to return to the Moon, and a robot rover or a careless visitor could drive across Neil Armstrong's first footprints or damage the Apollo landers. On Earth a government protects such a place by declaring it a park or a heritage site. Machu Picchu in Peru, for example, is protected through its host country and the World Heritage Convention. The Moon has no host country. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the basic international agreement on space, says no nation can take any part of the Moon by claiming it, using it or occupying it. A country that declared a park around a landing site would be doing something very close to what the treaty forbids.

So the Hanlons have tried to build protection out of other materials. Their first aim was a proposal for the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, the UN body that discusses space law and meets in Vienna, modelled on the World Heritage Convention. In December 2018 the UN General Assembly gave the group observer status on a provisional basis for three years, which lets it attend and speak at UN meetings without having a vote. It also approached companies directly, and the German firm PTScientists, then planning to send a rover to the Apollo 17 site, was the first to pledge support in public.

The second route was American law. In 2019 the group worked with the office of Senator Gary Peters on the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act. The Senate passed it unanimously on 18 July 2019, the House passed it in December 2020, and it became law on 31 December 2020. Its reach is narrow. It does not fence off any ground. It requires companies working with NASA on Moon missions to agree to follow NASA's guidelines on keeping away from American landing sites, guidelines that could not otherwise be enforced. It works as a condition of a contract, so a company with no NASA contract is untouched. Hanlon herself wrote that the pool of affected companies is small, and that its importance is that it was the first law of any nation to recognise human heritage in space.

The third route is promises between governments. Section 9 of the Artemis Accords, a US-led set of principles first signed by eight countries in October 2020, commits signers to preserve historic landing sites, artefacts and spacecraft. It was the first time such heritage appeared in an agreement among several countries, and 55 nations had signed by May 2025. In March 2021 the group released a free digital registry of historic landing sites, and in March 2023 it formed the Institute on Space Law and Ethics.

The case shows how someone can look after a place in space without owning it. Each protection binds only those who agreed to it, through a contract or a political promise. A country or company outside those arrangements has no duty under them, and China and Russia, which are building their own lunar plans, are not bound by the Artemis Accords.

gajardo-moon-chile.mechanism: A notary can record a statement about the Moon, but a country's land procedures reach only that country's land, and since 1967 no nation can claim the Moon at all.
gajardo-moon-chile.story:
Jenaro Gajardo Vera (1919 to 1998) was a Chilean lawyer, painter and poet who became known in his country as the legal owner of the Moon. He moved to the city of Talca, south of Santiago, in early 1951 to practise law. There he set up a group called the Interplanetary Telescopic Society, one of whose stated purposes was to form a welcoming committee for the first visitors from other worlds.

The Moon claim rests on a Chilean legal habit. At the time, a person holding land with no title deed could clean up the situation by declaring ownership "from before 1857" before a notary, an official who records that a statement was made. Gajardo said that on 25 September 1954 he went to the Talca notary César Jiménez Fuenzalida and used that exact formula. The wording he quoted says he owned the only natural satellite of the Earth, 3,475.99 kilometres across, and gives its boundaries as outer space to the north, south, east and west. Like any Chilean land filing, it also gives his street address and marital status.

He offered two reasons. One was a poetic protest, so he could have a say in who might one day live on the Moon, since he wanted a world free of envy, hatred and violence. The other was practical. The Talca Social Club admitted only members who owned property.

The details do not hold together well. Gajardo said the deed went into Talca's property registry, but the registry has no record of it. He also gave different dates at different times: 17 June 1956 in October 1968, 17 October 1956 in July 1969, and 16 July 1956 in November 1972. The story became public on 13 October 1968 in the newspaper La Nación, and the television host Don Francisco later interviewed him. A well-known tale says US President Richard Nixon wrote before the Apollo 11 landing in 1969 to ask his permission, and that Gajardo graciously agreed. No record of such a message exists.

The law gives the claim no support. A notary records that a person said something. Chile's procedure for land without deeds applied to land in Chile, and the Moon is not in Chile. From 1967 the Outer Space Treaty also barred any nation from claiming the Moon, so Chile could not have backed the deed even had it wished to. No authority ever bothered to challenge it. Gajardo died on 3 May 1998 and left the Moon to the Chilean people in his will. The case is included because it used a real legal procedure, and that procedure could not reach beyond Chile.

ilrs.mechanism: Two groups of countries are writing their own rules for Moon bases, one led by China and Russia and one by the United States. Each base keeps its own country's law inside it, and neither group gains ownership of the ground.

ilrs.story:
The International Lunar Research Station is a planned base on the Moon led by China and Russia, and its plans run in parallel with the American effort to return people to the Moon. It would stand on the surface or in lunar orbit and carry out scientific work and tests of technology, including long periods of running without people.

The two governments signed a memorandum, a written statement of intent, on 9 March 2021. On 16 June 2021 their space agencies, the China National Space Administration and Roscosmos, presented a roadmap at a conference in St Petersburg and described the project as open to all interested countries. That September they held closed talks on a draft declaration with experts from Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Malaysia, Thailand and the UN's space office. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was seen as ending the approach to European partners.

Membership then grew in a different direction. Venezuela signed on 17 July 2023, in a deal that also gave China access to Venezuelan ground stations for tracking and talking to spacecraft. South Africa followed on 1 September 2023, Azerbaijan on 3 October, and Pakistan and Belarus that same month. The University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates and the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization joined that November. Some partners are not governments. A Swiss company, Nano-SPACE, and a Hawaii-based nonprofit, the International Lunar Observatory Association, also signed. China announced a body to coordinate the work, the International Lunar Research Station Cooperation Organization, and a Xinhua report in April 2025 counted 17 countries and international organisations.

Construction missions are planned from 2031, using heavy rockets that are still being developed, the Chinese Long March 9 and the Russian Yenisei. Earlier robotic missions are meant to prepare the way. China's Chang'e 8, planned for 2028, is to test making useful materials from what is found on the Moon. In May 2025 a further memorandum set out a plan for a Russian nuclear power plant on the Moon by 2036 to power the base. None of the base has been built.

The legal position is the same as for any base on the Moon. Under Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty no country can claim the land beneath it. Under Article VIII each country keeps legal control over the objects it registers and the people working in them, so a Chinese module would be under Chinese authority and a Russian reactor under Russian authority, while the ground stayed unowned. Article XII of that treaty says stations on the Moon are to be open to visits from other parties. Partners in the project gain no territory by joining. They sign on to a shared plan, and what each one gets depends on its own agreement.

Two groups of countries are therefore writing practical rules for the Moon, this one and the American-led Artemis Accords. Which habits become normal on the Moon may depend on which group actually arrives and how it behaves.

lindsay-coles-early-deeds.mechanism: A notary's stamp and a clerk's entry record only that a person made a statement. They give no title, and no country's land system had authority over what was claimed.
lindsay-coles-early-deeds.story:
A. Dean Lindsay of Ocilla, a small town in Georgia, was one of the first Americans to claim objects in space by paper deed. He later described how it started. On a May night in 1936 he looked at the full moon, thought of it as real estate, said to himself that nobody owned it, and decided to acquire it with a deed of original claim.

On 15 June 1936 he went to a notary, an official who records that a statement was made, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He presented a claim to all planets, "islands-of-space" and other matter visible from Ocilla, to be known as "A.D. Lindsay's archapellago", with his spelling. He left out the Earth, reasoning that it belonged to those who live on it. He also first left out the Moon and Saturn, then claimed each in a separate deed. He sent the papers and the recording fee to the clerk of the Superior Court in Ocilla, who entered them on 28 June in Deed Book 11, pages 28 and 29, at the Irwin County Courthouse. Mental Floss gives the year of all this as 1937, while Futility Closet and Wikipedia give 1936. He had earlier made claims on the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

The clerk's act explains why such deeds looked real. A county clerk's job is to copy documents into the public record when a fee is paid, without deciding whether what they say is true. The deed was genuinely recorded, and that fact said nothing about whether Lindsay owned anything. Members of the public wrote offering to buy stars and constellations. He sent them all the same reply, that Henry Ford was not rich enough to buy them.

In the 1950s the idea became a business. Robert R. Coles, a former chairman of New York's Hayden Planetarium, started the Interplanetary Development Corporation and sold lots on the Moon at a dollar an acre.

The deeds are of the type called quitclaim, which pass on only whatever rights the seller may have, and promise nothing more. When the seller has no rights, the buyer receives none. All this happened about three decades before the 1967 Outer Space Treaty barred nations from claiming the Moon. Even before that, no country's land system reached the Moon, so no court had any way of enforcing a sale or removing a trespasser. No government or court ever tested these deeds.

lonestar-lunar-data.mechanism: Data stored on the Moon stays inside an object under the legal authority of a launching country, under Articles VI and VIII of the Outer Space Treaty. The company and its people also remain on Earth, within reach of courts there.
lonestar-lunar-data.story:
Lonestar Data Holdings is a company based in St Petersburg, Florida, that wants to run data centres on the Moon. A data centre is a building full of computers that store information for others. Lonestar's chief executive, Christopher Stott, gives two reasons for putting one on the Moon. The first is backup. Undersea cables get cut, and hurricanes, earthquakes and wars can destroy data, while the Moon has almost no weather. The company calls this resilience as a service.

The second reason is legal. More than 100 countries have data sovereignty laws, which restrict where certain data may be stored and processed, often to within the country itself. A company on Earth cannot satisfy all those countries from one place. Lonestar's pitch, as IEEE Spectrum, an engineering magazine, reported it, cites the 1967 Outer Space Treaty's statement that space and the Moon are not subject to national claims. A US spacecraft is under US law, the argument goes, but it could carry a sealed box under British law, or another country's, so one data centre could host many boxes for many customers.

The first test was called the Freedom Data Center. It weighed 1 kilogram, held 8 terabytes of solid-state storage in a 3D-printed case, and rode on the Athena lander built by the American company Intuitive Machines. It carried data for the Florida state government and the Isle of Man, along with a copy of the video game Starfield and a song from it. SpaceX launched the mission in late February 2025. On 6 March Athena reached the Mons Mouton area, about 5 degrees from the south pole, but it missed its target by more than 800 feet and came to rest on its side in a cold crater. The mission was declared over the next day. Lonestar told the TV station FOX 13 that its payload was intact and the only one to survive.

The legal idea has limits that the treaty itself sets. Article VI says each country bears international responsibility for what its companies do in space, and must authorise and keep supervising them. Article VIII says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal control over it, even on the Moon. So the data sits inside an object under the authority of some country on Earth, here the United States. The real attraction of the Moon for this purpose is narrower than being beyond all law. A customer may be able to choose which country's law applies to its box by contract, but a court or government can still reach the company, its staff and its offices on Earth. No court is known to have ruled on whether a box on the Moon satisfies a data-location law.

luna-2.mechanism: Scattering national emblems on the Moon creates no territory. The pieces remain property of the launching state, and the land stays unclaimed.
luna-2.story:
Luna 2 was a Soviet probe, launched on 12 September 1959, that crashed onto the Moon on purpose the next day. It was the first human-made object to reach another world, and it hit east of the plain called Mare Imbrium, near the craters Aristides, Archimedes and Autolycus. The position of about 29 degrees north is an estimate. The probe had no engine of its own and flew a direct path from its rocket.

Just before impact, two metal spheres carrying pentagonal shields engraved with "USSR" and the launch date were designed to burst and scatter the shields in all directions. In earlier centuries, a sailor who planted a flag on an empty shore could be part of a claim to that land, so these pennants raise an obvious question about ownership. The treaty that settled the matter came eight years afterwards.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, deals with this in two rules. Article II says no country can take the Moon by claim, use, occupation or any other means, so the ground around the pennants belongs to nobody. Article VIII says ownership of objects sent into space is not affected by their being there. A smashed probe therefore stays the property of whoever launched it, which today means Russia as the Soviet Union's continuing state. Anyone who wanted to collect the pieces would face a question about the objects and no question about the land.

luna-25.mechanism: Crashing does not end ownership. Debris on the Moon stays the property of the country that launched it, and the ground under it stays unclaimed.
luna-25.story:
Luna 25 was a Russian robotic lander, Russia's first Moon mission since the Soviet Luna 24 in 1976. It weighed 1,750 kilograms at launch and carried 30 kilograms of instruments, including a robotic arm to study the soil. It was meant to be the first craft to land near the Moon's south pole, and at least 12.5 billion rubles, over US$130 million, had been spent on it.

It lifted off on 10 August 2023 from the Vostochny launch site in Russia's Amur Region and reached lunar orbit on 16 August, with landing planned for 21 August near Boguslawsky crater. On 19 August an engine firing meant to change its orbit went wrong, and its new path ran into the surface. It struck the inner rim of Pontécoulant G crater at 11:57 UTC, about 400 kilometres short of where it was meant to land. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter later found the impact site.

A wreck on the Moon raises the question of whether it can be treated like a ship abandoned at sea. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says a spacecraft stays under the legal authority of the country that registered it, and that its being on another world does not change who owns it, including its parts. The article sets no time limit and makes no exception for crashes. So the debris remains Russian property, and another country's later mission could not simply claim it. Russia also gained nothing on the ground, since Article II bars any country from claiming the land the wreck lies on.

lunar-embassy.mechanism: The UN's failure to reply gave Hope no ownership. Legal experts read the Outer Space Treaty's ban as reaching private claims too, because a private title needs a state to enforce it and no state may claim the Moon.
lunar-embassy.story:
Lunar Embassy is a company that sells deeds to land on the Moon and other planets, run by Dennis Hope, an entrepreneur in Nevada. It is the best known of the firms that sell space real estate, and its story turns on a reading of one sentence in a treaty.

In 1980 Hope was going through a divorce and was out of money. By his own account he thought that owning property might help, looked out of a window at the Moon, and went to a library. There he read the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, whose Article II says outer space, including the Moon, is not subject to national appropriation. Hope concluded that the treaty stopped only nations, so that the Moon was unowned land open to a private person. He filed a claim of ownership to the Moon, the other planets and their moons, and sent it to the United Nations with a note saying he meant to subdivide and sell it and asking them to tell him of any legal problem. They never replied, and he treats that silence as approval.

He has sold deeds full time since 1995. The product is a printed deed with the buyer's name. In 2009 National Geographic reported $22.49 an acre plus tax. Discover magazine reported more than $9 million in sales to 4.25 million people at $19.99 a sale. In an interview with Vice, Hope claimed 611 million acres sold on the Moon, 325 million on Mars and 125 million on Venus, Io and Mercury, and he priced a continent-sized plot of 5,332,740 acres at $13,331,000, which he said no one had yet bought. By his own figures 17 percent of buyers see it as a novelty. Most of these numbers come from Hope himself.

In 2001, he says, 163,000 customers emailed to ask how their property would be protected. His answer was a Galactic Government, whose constitution he says took three years to write, went online in March 2004, and was ratified by 173,562 votes. It claims a congress, a patent office and a currency that he says is backed by helium-3, a rare gas in the lunar soil. He describes it as a sovereign nation. No country is known to treat it as one.

Space lawyers reject the argument behind all this. Tanja Masson-Zwaan, then president of the International Institute of Space Law, said the treaty applies to governments and to their private citizens, which defeats Hope's claim. The reason is that Article VI makes each country answerable for what its people do in space. A private owner needs some government's courts to enforce the title, and any country that enforced it would be exercising the kind of claim Article II forbids. Ram Jakhu, a law professor at McGill University in Canada, said he saw no loophole and that no one can own property in outer space. As for the UN's silence, legal experts told National Geographic that the UN did not answer because it did not have to, since the Moon cannot be claimed under the treaty.

No government has ruled on the deeds, and the company's website was still selling them in 2026. A buyer gets a contract with a seller and a piece of paper. By Hope's own account, the buyer does not even get the right to stop others landing on the plot, since the treaty lets all nations explore.

lunar-registry.mechanism: Selling deeds to land that cannot be claimed creates a contract between buyer and seller. It transfers nothing on the Moon, and no recording method, whether a library or a blockchain, changes that.
lunar-registry.story:
The Official Lunar Registry is a private website that sells deeds to acres on the Moon, a rival to Dennis Hope's Lunar Embassy. Its site says it has operated since 1999 with more than 125,000 customers, under a body called the International Lunar Lands Administration together with Luna Society International. The names sound official. They are the seller's own, and no government is involved. The people who run it personally are not named on the site.

The business has changed its pitch over time. An article in GOOD magazine described a stated mission of funding private exploration and settlement, with people living permanently on the Moon by 2015, and said deeds cost between 20 and 30 dollars an acre. Buyers chose a place from a moon atlas, such as the Sea of Cold or the Sea of Clouds, whose areas were zoned for tourism, housing, science and business. The deeds were said to be copyrighted and deposited at the US Library of Congress and other libraries and offices. Copyright protects the wording of a document from being copied. Depositing a copy in a library says nothing about whether the document's claims are true, and neither act has any bearing on who owns land. No settlement followed.

In 2011 Gizmodo reported that it called itself Earth's leading lunar real-estate agency and charged about $20 an acre. By 2026 the site offered land starting under US$20, with real lunar coordinates, an elegant certificate and an ownership contract recorded on the Ethereum blockchain, a shared digital ledger, through the marketplace OpenSea. The same site also calls the purchase a keepsake. A blockchain entry proves that a certain record was made at a certain time. It does not make the record true, in the same way that a notary's stamp does not.

The site also lists "Lunar Republic" as a trademark, a phrase from Robert Heinlein's 1949 story The Man Who Sold the Moon.

Stephen Doyle, a retired NASA official, told Gizmodo that people may go and take lunar soil but have no right to draw a square on the surface and call it theirs. He said a governing body would be needed to recognise and enforce property rights on the Moon, and none exists, so such claims are not much more than fancy paper. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 bars nations from claiming the Moon, and no court is known to have tested these deeds. A buyer's only clear rights are those in the contract with the seller.

moon-agreement.mechanism: A treaty binds only the countries that join it. The one treaty making the Moon's resources common property has few members, and countries that want to mine have stayed out or left.
moon-agreement.story:
The Moon Agreement is the UN treaty that treats the Moon's resources as belonging to all humanity, and it is the one space treaty most countries have refused. To follow why, it helps to know where it sits. Between 1967 and 1979 UN members concluded five treaties on space, starting with the Outer Space Treaty, which says no country can claim the Moon. That treaty says little about mining. The Moon Agreement was meant to fill the gap.

Argentina, Poland and France raised the idea in the UN's space committee in 1969, and the Soviet Union circulated a draft in May 1971. An American memorandum of that September, since declassified, says the US view was that the Soviet proposal largely repeated the 1967 treaty and was offered as a way to use up committee time, and that the United States would support it. The UN General Assembly adopted the agreement on 5 December 1979, and it took effect on 11 July 1984.

The core is Article 11. It repeats that no one can claim the Moon, and allows collecting samples. It then calls the Moon's resources the common heritage of mankind, and commits members to set up an international system to govern mining once mining is about to become possible. That system is meant to manage the resources sensibly and share the benefits equitably, with special consideration for countries that contributed to exploring the Moon. The same model is used for the deep seabed, where the International Seabed Authority manages mining under the Law of the Sea. For someone planning a settlement or a mine, the difference is large. Under the 1967 treaty a company might hope to keep what it digs up. Under this one, an international body would have a say and a share.

That is the reason for most of the opposition. In the United States, campaigners from the L5 Society, a group of space settlement enthusiasts, fought the treaty in 1979 and 1980, arguing that common heritage would stifle development. The United States and the Soviet Union did not join, and neither has any other leading space power. The US later issued an executive order stating that it rejects the agreement, on the grounds that legal uncertainty was discouraging companies.

A treaty binds only the countries that join it. The UN treaty database lists 17 members, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Chile, Mexico, the Netherlands and Pakistan. France, Guatemala, India and Romania signed but never ratified. Saudi Arabia joined on 18 July 2012, signed the US-led Artemis Accords on 14 July 2022, and notified the UN on 5 January 2023 that it was leaving, the first withdrawal from any of the five space treaties. Its exit took effect on 5 January 2024. For All Moonkind and others suggested it wanted freedom to mine under national law.

The treaty remains in force for its members, and the international mining system has never been set up. Mining itself has not yet begun, so the promise in Article 11 has not yet come due.

moon-express-faa.mechanism: The United States met its Article VI duty for this lunar mission through an improvised review by an aviation regulator, because no dedicated law existed. Any private space venture needs a state willing to authorise and supervise it.
moon-express-faa.story:
Moon Express is a private American company formed in August 2010 by Robert Richards, Naveen Jain and Barney Pell. It worked from the NASA Ames Research Center in California, and it aimed to win the $30 million Google Lunar XPRIZE, a contest for the first private landing on the Moon, and in the long run to mine the Moon for metals that are rare on Earth. Its small robot lander, the MX-1E, was about the size of a coffee table.

The company's problem in 2016 was legal. Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty permits private activity in space but says it requires "authorization and continuing supervision" by the company's own country. Suppose an American firm wants to land on the Moon. The United States has promised the world it will authorise and watch over that firm. Yet US law at the time had no office for this. The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, passed after the first private company sought clearance to launch in 1982, gave the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) power over launches and returns to Earth. Nothing covered what a craft did after it left Earth orbit. Investors want to know that a mission is lawful, and a launch provider needs a licence.

So Moon Express asked the FAA for a payload review, a check on what a rocket is carrying. On 20 July 2016 the FAA gave a favourable payload determination, announced on 3 August, the first for a commercial payload intended to land on the Moon. It made the decision in consultation with the State Department and NASA, and found no threat to public safety, national security, foreign policy or US international obligations, including Article IV of the treaty, which says the Moon is to be used only for peaceful purposes. The company's chief executive called it a landmark. A similar letter had gone to Bigelow Aerospace in December 2014 about a future inflatable base on the Moon.

Lawyers saw a stopgap. Berin Szóka of the group TechFreedom said the law covered only launch and re-entry, and the FAA was stretching that power to reach activity on the Moon. Such letters would not bind a future agency, he said, and it was unclear whether they would satisfy Article VI if another country challenged them. He urged Congress to pass a clear law.

The mission never flew. No team in the contest launched by the deadline of 31 March 2018, and from late 2018 the company turned to supporting NASA's commercial delivery programme. Its activity after 2020 is not known. The case matters because it shows the plumbing behind any private venture in space. Even a company that claims no land needs a government willing to answer for it, and that government must find some legal way to do so.

shackleton-south-pole.mechanism: No country can own the lunar south pole, however useful its ice. Whoever arrives first gets control of their own machines and no rights over the land, and the treaty gives no clear rule for a spot two countries both want.
shackleton-south-pole.story:
Shackleton is a crater at the Moon's south pole, named after the Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton. The pole itself lies on its rim. It is 21 kilometres across and 4.2 kilometres deep, and it marks the region that both the United States and China want to reach.

Its value comes from an accident of geometry. The Moon's axis is tilted so little that sunlight at the pole comes in sideways. Peaks on the rim are lit for about 80 to 90 percent of each lunar orbit, which makes them attractive places for solar panels. The crater floor never sees the Sun and is extremely cold, so water and other substances that arrive may freeze and stay there. Readings from the Lunar Prospector spacecraft showed more hydrogen than usual in the crater, which may point to water ice. Ice could support human outposts or be turned into rocket fuel. Sunny peaks and shadowed floors lie close together here, which is why several countries want the same small area.

Both powers are aiming here. NASA named nine candidate landing regions around the pole in October 2024. In 2026 it changed its plan, so that Artemis III became a test in Earth orbit in 2027 and crews would land on Artemis IV and V in 2028, with the pole still the destination. China's Chang'e 7, with an orbiter, lander, rover and a small hopping probe, is planned to land on Shackleton's sunlit rim, search for ice and scout a site for the International Lunar Research Station, the base China and Russia announced in 2021. It was rolled to the launch pad on 19 August 2026, but its launch was called off because it did not meet launch conditions, and it is now expected in 2027.

The law gives no one this ground. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, bars any country from claiming the Moon by use or occupation, so the first to land does not gain the crater. Article VIII gives a country control over its own machines and crews only. The hard question is what happens when one country's base sits on the best peak. Article IX requires states to act with due regard to the interests of others, and the treaty gives no rule for who gets a spot that two countries both want. The US-led Artemis Accords provide for temporary safety zones, in which signers announce their activities and coordinate to avoid interference, while promising to respect free access for others. Critics argue the Accords conflict with the ban on national claims. Nothing has landed at this site, so the question has not been tested.

slim.mechanism: Legal authority over a spacecraft does not end when the mission does. A dead lander stays under the country that registered it, and the land under it remains no one's.
slim.why: Corrected last contact: the entry said April 2024, but the source says SLIM woke on 23 April after its third lunar night and went silent in late May 2024.
slim.story:
SLIM, the Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, was a Japanese robot lander nicknamed the Moon Sniper. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) built it to show that a craft could land within 100 metres of its target. Apollo 11's landing area had been an oval 20 kilometres long. It found its way by recognising craters, with methods borrowed from face-recognition software, and it cost an expected 18 billion yen, about US$121.5 million.

It launched on 6 September 2023 and touched down near Shioli crater in the Sea of Nectar on 19 January 2024, making Japan the fifth country to land softly on the Moon. It came down on its side with its solar panels facing away from the Sun, so it was shut down the next day on battery power. It woke nine days later, when the sunlight moved round to the panels. It had not been designed to survive the bitter cold of the two-week lunar night, yet it did so three times, waking on 23 April 2024 after the third. It went silent in late May, and JAXA declared the mission over on 23 August 2024.

The silent spacecraft is still Japanese. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it while it is in space or on another world, and that ownership does not change. The article sets no end date tied to the life of a mission. A dead lander is like a parked car in one respect, since nobody else may take it just because it has stopped working. The ground under it stays unclaimed.

unreal-estate-pop.mechanism: Pop argues that the Outer Space Treaty closes off private land claims in space, because no state could lawfully recognise them. His mock claim on the Sun shows that anyone can produce such a paper.
unreal-estate-pop.story:
Virgiliu Pop is a Romanian space lawyer, born in 1974, who wrote the main history of private claims to the Moon. He works for the Romanian Space Agency and is a member of the International Institute of Space Law. He wrote a doctoral thesis at the University of Glasgow in Scotland on rights to land in outer space. He then published Unreal Estate: The Men Who Sold the Moon in 2006, and a later book on land and mineral ownership beyond Earth in 2009.

Unreal Estate shows how old and how varied these claims are. Pop traces them back 250 years to Prussia, where King Frederick was said to have granted the Moon to a farmer with healing powers. That story surfaced only in the 1990s, when a descendant, Martin Juergens of Germany, contested Dennis Hope's claims, with a date given of 15 July 1756. In the 1940s people wrote to the US Bureau of Land Management asking about homesteads on the Moon. In the 1950s deeds for square inches of Moon came free with breakfast cereal, and in the 1960s several towns officially annexed the Moon and Venus.

Pop sorts claimants into groups. Some sell acres for money, with Hope's Lunar Embassy the best known. Others raised funds for museums, planetariums and, in one case, a school sports complex in Romania. Some were jokes, such as BuyUranus.com. A few tried to test the law, such as Greg Nemitz, who claimed the asteroid Eros and sought US government recognition of it. Pop reported that several million people held such certificates.

In his final chapter he takes apart Hope's argument with several lines of reasoning. Others had filed claims to the Moon before Hope, so even on Hope's own theory he would not be first. Any government that recognised such a claim would be in conflict with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars nations from claiming the Moon. And the claimants lack the physical ability to hold the land, which is what land law has traditionally asked of a first claimant. He says such claims are a trivial issue for space lawyers, yet they have shaped the public's view of space law.

To make his point he himself claimed ownership of the Sun, a claim he says is as bogus as the others. He has also argued that the Moon is a commons, a thing shared by all, while predicting that this status would not last if mining the Moon became practical.

fonuafoou-falcon-island.mechanism: Volcanic land can appear and vanish at the same spot. Under Article 121 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a place counts as an island only while it stays above water at high tide.
fonuafoou-falcon-island.story:
Fonuafoʻou, meaning "new land" in Tongan, is an undersea volcano in the western Haʻapai group of Tonga, a Pacific kingdom of scattered islands. It has built an island above the waves several times and lost it each time.

The crew of the British ship HMS Falcon spotted the site in 1867, when it was a coral reef. On 11 October 1885 the volcano erupted, and three days later an island stood there, which the British named Falcon Island. Eruptions in 1894, 1921, 1927, 1928, 1933 and 1936 built it up, and by 1949 it was reported at 6 kilometres across and 145 metres high. That year another eruption blew the island apart and it collapsed under the sea. There were further eruptions in 1970 and 1993, and the top now lies 17 metres below the surface.

The law of the sea explains why such a place is hard to rely on. Article 121 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets out states' rights at sea, defines an island as a naturally formed area of land, surrounded by water, which is above water at high tide. An island can generate rights over surrounding sea, while a rock under the surface generates none of its own. Falcon Island met that test for about 64 years on and off, and now it does not. Suppose a group had settled the 1949 island and declared a country. They would have lost the ground under their feet in a single eruption, and with it the thing a state most needs, which is territory. This volcano also sits among Tongan islands, where Tonga's own name for it is the one now used.

graham-island-ferdinandea.mechanism: New land in the sea can attract rival claims within weeks. These four were never settled, because the island wore away after about six months and left nothing to decide.
graham-island-ferdinandea.story:
Graham Island was a volcanic island that rose from the Mediterranean about 30 kilometres south of Sicily in July 1831 and sank again within six months. It is the top of an undersea volcano called Empedocles, which has broken the surface four or five times in recorded history, going back to the 3rd century BC. It is also the best known case of countries rushing to claim land that then disappeared.

The first signs came in late June 1831, when two Royal Navy ships felt an earthquake between Sciacca, a town on the Sicilian coast, and the island of Pantelleria. In early July a smell of sulphur spread through Sciacca. On 12 July a captain from Naples reported smoke rising from the sea, and another ship's captain saw bubbling water. People watching from shore thought it might be a ferry on fire.

By 17 July there was enough land for a Sicilian customs official, Michele Fiorini, to step ashore and plant an oar to claim it for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, the state then ruling southern Italy and Sicily. The location explains the interest that followed. It sat near the main shipping routes between Sicily and North Africa, closer to Europe than Britain's base at Malta. On 2 August Captain Humphrey Senhouse of the Royal Navy planted the Union Jack and named it after Sir James Graham, head of the Admiralty. King Ferdinand II sent the warship Etna to claim it and name it Ferdinandea. The French geologist Constant Prévost named it Julia, because it was born in July. Spain also declared an interest, which made four rival claimants.

In July and August it reached about 4 square kilometres and 63 metres high, with two small lakes. Tourists came to see it, and nobles reportedly thought of a holiday resort. The diplomats argued. The island was made of tephra, loose volcanic ash and fragments, and once the eruption stopped, the waves cut it down. Officials reported no trace of it by 17 December, and the dispute lapsed unsettled with nothing left to decide.

The summit reappeared briefly in 1863 and now lies about 6 metres under water, marked on charts as a danger to ships. When it showed signs of activity in 2000 and 2002, Italians placed a flag and a marble plaque on the bank to head off future claims, which indicates that the old quarrel is still remembered. In today's law of the sea, a state's rights over a nearby undersea bank depend on where it lies relative to coasts, so the question would be argued differently. The 1831 episode shows how fast claims form when new land has strategic value, and how quickly loose ash can remove the subject of a dispute.

hunga-tonga-new-island.mechanism: Under Article 121 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, land formed naturally and standing above high tide counts as an island. It keeps that status only as long as it stays above the water.
hunga-tonga-new-island.story:
Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai is an undersea volcano in Tonga, in the South Pacific, about 65 kilometres north of Tonga's main island, Tongatapu. It rises about 2,000 metres from the seabed, and its only large parts above water were two small uninhabited islands, Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai, which sit on the rim of its sunken crater. They were about 1.6 kilometres apart, each around 2 kilometres long.

An eruption in 2014 and 2015 piled up a new cone that joined them into one island. A strip of deposits 380 metres wide, called a tombolo, linked the new ground to its neighbour. The highest point reached 149 metres. Scientists first expected it to wash away soon, as most such islands do, but it lasted about seven years. Surveys in 2019 found ferns, guava trees, mosses and sedges, along with cockroaches, hermit crabs, moths, rats and spiders, and seabirds were breeding there.

For the law, the question is what new land counts as. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets out states' rights at sea, defines an island in Article 121 as land formed naturally, surrounded by water and above high tide. This ground met that test. It also rose among islands already held by Tonga, so it offered no empty land for anyone else to claim.

In January 2022 the volcano erupted again, the largest eruption of the 21st century so far, sending a plume 58 kilometres high and a tsunami as far as Japan and the Americas. The explosion destroyed most of the joined island and separated the two pieces again, and only small remnants are left. Anyone who had built on the new ground in those seven years would have lost it in a day, along with the living plants and animals. An island's legal status lasts only as long as the land does.

nishinoshima-growth.mechanism: When new land grows onto an island a state already holds, it adds to that state's territory, so no separate question of ownership arises.
nishinoshima-growth.story:
Nishinoshima is a volcanic island belonging to Japan, about 940 kilometres south-southeast of Tokyo and 130 kilometres west of Chichijima, the nearest inhabited island in the Ogasawara chain. Spanish sailors on the ship Rosario found it in 1702, and it carried the name Rosario Island until Japan made Nishinoshima, meaning West Island, its official name in 1904. Until 1973 it was a small green island about 650 metres long, with no eruptions in the past 10,000 years, and only the tip of an undersea volcano about 3,000 metres high.

On 30 May 1973 the crew of a fishing boat told the Japan Coast Guard they had seen white smoke rising near the island. The Coast Guard flew over the same day and kept watching from the air. By September a new island had formed with a cone about 40 metres high. By August 1974 the new land was put at about 316,000 square metres, and erosion and shifting sand then joined it to the old island. For a time it had been called Nishinoshima Shintō, the New Island, but once joined it was no longer treated as separate.

A further eruption began in November 2013 and built another islet to the southeast. Officials said they would name it after it was stable and clearly going to stay. It merged with the main island first, and an official said there was little chance it would be named separately. By July 2016 a cone stood about 142 metres high. More eruptions followed, and by August 2020 the island was about 4.1 kilometres across, with plants and animals returning.

This case shows how a state handles new land when it is already on the spot. A Japanese agency watched each stage, Japanese officials decided about names, and the new ground grew onto an island Japan already held. No other country is recorded as claiming it, and no private group could have used it as an opening. The land simply extended existing Japanese territory, in the way that land added by a river to the bank of someone's farm becomes part of that farm.

south-talpatti-new-moore.mechanism: A sandbar too low and unstable to settle can still matter because it might move a sea boundary. An arbitration tribunal, a panel of judges chosen to settle a dispute, ruled on this one's position after it had gone under the sea.
south-talpatti-new-moore.story:
South Talpatti, which India called New Moore and also Purbasha, was a low sandbar in the Bay of Bengal, claimed by both India and Bangladesh. Nobody ever lived on it, and it never stood more than 2 metres above the sea, yet the two countries argued over it for decades.

It formed from silt after the Bhola cyclone of November 1970, in the huge delta where the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers reach the sea. A US satellite picked it up in 1974 at about 2,500 square metres. It later grew to about 10,000 square metres at low tide. There was speculation that oil and gas lay in the area.

The reason for the quarrel lay in an old border rule. When British India was divided in 1947, the Radcliffe Award set the boundary, and on rivers the border follows the middle of the main channel, a rule known as the thalweg. The sandbar lay only 2 kilometres from the mouth of the Hariabhanga River, which marks the border between the two countries. If the main channel ran to the east of the sandbar, it was on India's side, and if to the west, on Bangladesh's. India said its 1981 survey showed the deep channel on the east, and similar data appeared on British and American charts. Bangladesh said its data showed the main flow on the west. Delta channels also move over time, so it could matter which year was used.

Possession was mostly symbolic. India reportedly raised its flag in 1981 and set up a temporary Border Security Force base, visiting with gunboats. Neither country built anything lasting, because the delta floods every year and reshapes the ground. The stakes were out at sea. The location of the sandbar might have affected where the two countries' sea boundary ran, and with it who controlled the seabed resources offshore.

In October 2009 Bangladesh took the wider sea boundary dispute to the Permanent Court of Arbitration, a body where a panel of judges chosen under agreed rules settles a dispute between states. In March 2010 Sugata Hazra, an Indian oceanographer at Jadavpur University, reported that the island had disappeared, and named sea level rise, shifting river flows and sinking land as causes. The final award of 7 July 2014, which cannot be appealed, gave Bangladesh 19,467 of the 25,000 square kilometres of disputed sea, and placed the site of the vanished sandbar on India's side. So Bangladesh won most of the water and India won a patch of sea where an island had been.

The case shows that even a useless strip of sand can matter when it might move a boundary at sea. It also shows that the sea rights, once fixed by judges, can outlast the land that started the argument.

surtsey-paris-match.mechanism: New land off a coastal state's shore is treated as that state's from the start. The state can then close it with a conservation order before anyone settles.
surtsey-paris-match.story:
Surtsey is a volcanic island off the south coast of Iceland, in the Vestmannaeyjar group, and it is now Iceland's southernmost point. It formed from an eruption that began 130 metres below the sea, and it is one of the few new islands of modern times that has lasted.

The first signs were weak tremors recorded in early November 1963. On 13 November a fishing boat noted warmer water. At 07:15 on 14 November the cook of the trawler Ísleifur II saw a column of dark smoke. The captain thought a boat might be on fire and went to look, and the crew found explosions of black ash breaking the surface. Within days the new island was more than 500 metres long. An Icelandic naming committee called it Surtsey, after Surtr, a fire giant in Norse myth.

On 6 December 1963 three French journalists from the magazine Paris Match landed and stayed about 15 minutes until explosions drove them off. They jokingly claimed the island for France, and Iceland quickly stated that it belonged to Iceland. The joke touches a real rule. New land rising just off a country's coast comes up in water that country already controls, so a foreign visitor who plants a flag acquires nothing.

By early 1964 the island was big enough to keep the sea from reaching the vents, so the explosions gave way to lava flows. That lava capped the loose ash, which is why Surtsey survived where neighbours such as Jólnir washed away. The eruption lasted until 5 June 1967, by which point the island covered 2.7 square kilometres. Waves have since cut it to 1.3 square kilometres by 2012. Scientists estimate it will stay above the sea until at least 2100.

Iceland's next step shows how a state can close off a new place. In 1965, with the eruption still going on, it declared Surtsey a nature reserve so that scientists could watch life arrive on bare rock without interference. The first flowering plant, a sea rocket, was found in spring 1965. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2008. Only a few scientists may land, and everyone else can see it closely only from a small plane. No one has been able to settle there, and an attempt would be a matter for Icelandic law and police.
