zalzala-koh.mechanism: A coastal state owns the seabed under its territorial sea, the belt of water next to its coast, under Article 2 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Land rising 2 kilometres offshore therefore comes up on that state's own territory.
zalzala-koh.story:
Zalzala Koh was a small island that appeared in the Arabian Sea off Pakistan on 24 September 2013, within hours of a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in the province of Balochistan. Its name means Earthquake Mountain in Urdu, and it was also called Earthquake Island. It stood about 2 kilometres from shore, off the Gwadar and Hingol coast, close enough to be seen from land.

It was probably not rock pushed up by the quake. It may have been a mud volcano, a mound of mud forced up by gas underground. The head of Pakistan's National Institute of Oceanography said gas escaping from the seabed had caused it. Satellite measurements put it at about 175 metres long, 160 metres wide and 15 to 20 metres high, though those figures were debated. The surface was lifeless, but fish and coral gathered around it, which helped local fishing.

Geologists predicted it would not last. It sank 3 metres within a month and had gone by the end of 2016.

Its legal position was simple and leaves no room for a new country. Under Article 2 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal state's rule extends over its territorial sea, a belt of water up to 12 nautical miles wide, including the seabed beneath it. Land rising 2 kilometres from shore comes up on the state's own territory, in the same way that a new hill on someone's farm belongs to the farm. Had anyone tried to camp on it and declare independence, Pakistan's ordinary law would have applied from the start.

global-country-of-world-peace.mechanism: Buying land gives a private owner title to it, while the country it lies in keeps governing it. Sovereignty, the right to govern a territory, has to be granted by a state, and every state the group approached refused.
global-country-of-world-peace.story:
The Global Country of World Peace is a non-profit organisation that calls itself a world government without borders. Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, the Indian founder of Transcendental Meditation, launched it on 7 October 2000 as "a country without borders for peace-loving people everywhere". It was incorporated in the US state of Iowa in 2002, with headquarters in Maharishi Vedic City, Iowa, and has centres in the United States, the Netherlands and Ireland. Its tax filings describe its mission as creating world peace by unifying all nations in happiness, prosperity, invincibility and perfect health, and it planned "palaces of peace" in 3,000 of the world's major cities.

Its structure imitates a kingdom. The neurologist Tony Nader was named its First Sovereign Ruler in 2000, later taking the title Maharaja. Rajas, or kings, are initiates said to hold spiritual authority over an existing nation. In 2005, 22 were appointed after a two-month course, and they were advised to contribute $1,000,000 to the Maharishi World Peace Fund. They wear white silk robes and gold crowns. A website lists ministers in departments such as Defence and Finance.

What makes it a useful case is its attempts to get real sovereignty, meaning the right to govern a territory as a state does. A private group can buy land, but only a state can give up its own rule over part of it, so the group approached governments. In November 2000 it offered Suriname $1.3 billion over three years for a 200-year lease of 3,500 acres, plus 1 percent of the money the new state's central bank put into circulation and a promise of 10,000 jobs. No deal followed. In July 2001 the island nation of Tuvalu rejected, after serious consideration, a Vatican-style city-state near its airport in exchange for $2 million a year. In 2002 Rota, in the US-linked Northern Mariana Islands, declined a request for 100 acres. In Costa Rica the group allegedly offered families on the Talamanca reservation $250 a month for the right to appoint a king, and a ceremony named a local man king. The Security Minister saw this as an attempt at an independent state and ordered its representative out of the country.

The group did own ordinary property, including a 30-acre island in Ireland and more than 1,000 acres near Smith Center, Kansas, where a national capital was planned in 2006. All of it stayed under the law of the country concerned, so buying land gave it what any landowner gets and no more.

It also issued a currency, the raam, printed by a Dutch firm in notes of 1, 5 and 10, with one raam set at 10 euros or 10 dollars. It was described as a bearer bond, which pays whoever holds it. By one estimate $40,000 worth was circulating in 2002, in Iowa, and more than 100 Dutch shops accepted it. That shows private money can work among willing users, and it did not make the issuer a state. The group continues, under Nader, with no territory of its own.

nova-roma.mechanism: Calling a group a sovereign nation has no legal effect when it holds no territory. In law Nova Roma is a non-profit organisation registered in Maine.
nova-roma.story:
Nova Roma, meaning New Rome, is an international non-profit organisation that aims to restore the religion, culture and values of ancient Rome. It was formed in 1998 and later incorporated in the US state of Maine, which is its only legal form. It offers a living community for re-enactors, scholars and fans of ancient Rome, and people who regard themselves as Romans today.

It is built like the Roman Republic, with a senate, elected officials and laws passed by the votes of members, and it calls itself a sovereign nation. Latin is its official language. Ancient Roman religion is its state religion, with priestly offices restored and the Roman holidays observed, alongside a guarantee of religious freedom. Groups in different countries can form local branches called provinces. It minted coins in 2000 and 2005. Daily activity means conventions, online games, a literary contest for historical novels, and appearances at history festivals in places such as Bulgaria, Hungary, Italy and Wells, Maine. It marked its twentieth anniversary at the festival of Rome's founding in Rome itself.

Some outside observers class it as a micronation, a small self-declared state that other states do not recognise. The label fits only loosely, since it claims no territory. Its citizens go on living and paying taxes under the laws of their own countries, and its laws work like the rules of a club, which bind members only as long as they choose to stay. Its present level of activity has not been confirmed. Its inclusion shows that a state's forms, such as a senate, coins and citizens, can exist without the land and power that make a state in law.

nutopia.mechanism: A declaration alone gives no one diplomatic immunity, because that protection comes from the state hosting a diplomat. Lennon's position changed only when US authorities overturned the deportation order in 1975.
nutopia.story:
Nutopia was a country with no land, announced by the musician John Lennon and the artist Yoko Ono at a press conference in New York City on 2 April 1973, the day after they signed its declaration. The name combines "new" and "utopia". It began as a response to a practical problem.

Lennon was trying to stay in the United States. Ono had a green card, the US permit for permanent residence, but Lennon had been refused one, and the week before the press conference he had received an order to leave the country. The couple's answer used humour. The declaration says Nutopia has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people, and no laws other than cosmic ones. Anyone could become a citizen by declaring awareness of it. As its two ambassadors, Lennon and Ono asked for diplomatic immunity, the legal protection foreign diplomats have from a host country's courts and immigration rules, along with recognition at the United Nations.

The trappings were jokes with a point. At the press conference Lennon waved a white handkerchief and called it the flag, saying it stood for surrender to peace and love. The New York Times reporter said he then blew his nose on it. The anthem, on Lennon's 1973 album Mind Games, is four seconds of silence. The Great Seal is a drawing of a seal balancing a globe on its nose. The embassy was first an apartment at 1 White Street in Manhattan, home of friends and the headquarters of the committee helping with the immigration case, and later a gold plaque on the kitchen back door of their apartment at the Dakota building.

Diplomatic immunity does not work by asking for it. A diplomat receives protection because a sending state exists, and the host state has accepted that person. The United States had no reason to accept envoys from a country it did not recognise, and no government is known to have granted the request. Lennon's status changed through ordinary law. The deportation order was overturned in 1975, and he received his green card in 1976.

In 2009 a New York exhibit showed the founding letter. Since April 2024 people have been able to declare citizenship through a website, promoted from Ono's account on X. Its population is unknown, because not all citizenships have been recorded. The case shows a declaration used as protest and publicity, and it had neither land nor legal effect.

obsidia.mechanism: A territory that fits in a briefcase is a claim that travels with objects. The law of whichever country the briefcase is in continues to apply to the people carrying it.
obsidia.story:
The Ambulatory Free States of Obsidia is a feminist micronation, a small self-declared state that no government recognises, founded in 2015 by Karo Yagjian, who holds the title Grand Marshal. Its whole territory is two slabs of obsidian, a black volcanic rock, each about the size of a book, carried in an electric blue and hot pink briefcase usually kept in Oakland, California. Its website warns that humans cannot physically enter the landmass.

Yagjian describes it as a fun art project that is also serious. As a teenager she learned of Neue Slowenische Kunst, a Slovenian art collective that has claimed since 1991 to be a state, issuing passports and stamps. That showed her, she says, how temporary state authority can be. In 2015 she heard of MicroCon, a summit of micronations started by the Republic of Molossia in Nevada, due to meet in Anaheim, California. She did not want to attend as a spectator, so she took a chunk of obsidian from a pile belonging to a man she was seeing and declared independence.

Its working life is small and playful. There is a national anthem, state animals (snails and swans), national sports (sailing and croquet) and a navy of two sailboats and a dinghy. It has no agreed currency, and accepts barter, fruit and American dollars. Each 4 July citizens burn their own flag on what they call Destroy Nationalism Day, and Swansmas falls on 27 December. To become a citizen, a person faces the flag, gives the salute and swears to uphold Obsidia's values until they die or become bored. Anyone can join, but cisgender men cannot serve in the government, which had eight officials. In November 2021 Huck magazine reported about 250 citizens, roughly 50 with passports, which are not required and serve more as conversation starters, and embassies in Hong Kong and Germany. Its present activity has not been confirmed.

Its politics are anti-capitalist, feminist and opposed to borders. One official sails with Women on Waves, a group that provides abortion services outside territorial waters. In legal terms the briefcase is ordinary luggage. It sits under the law of whichever country it is in, and carrying it across a border gives its holder none of the rights of a diplomat or a state. The project uses that point deliberately, by asking what makes a country at all.

bishop-ring.mechanism: Under Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the state that registers an object sent into space keeps legal control over it. However large it was, a habitat like this would still count as one space object under the law of the state that registered it.
bishop-ring.story:
The Bishop Ring is a design for an enormous space habitat, a place built for people to live in space permanently. Picture a giant wheel in space, turning steadily, with people living on the inside of the rim. The turning presses everything outward against the rim, and to the people there it feels like gravity. Forrest Bishop of the Institute of Atomic-Scale Engineering proposed it in 1997.

Earlier designs from the 1970s, by Gerard O'Neill and NASA, assumed steel, which limited how large a spinning structure could be before it tore itself apart. Bishop proposed carbon nanotubes, an extremely strong material made of carbon atoms, and scaled up accordingly. The ring would have a radius of about 1,000 kilometres and a width of 500 kilometres, giving about 3 million square kilometres of living space, close to the area of Argentina or India. At that scale it would need no roof. The artificial gravity would hold the air down against the rim, and walls about 200 kilometres high along the edges would keep it from spilling off. Mirrors or an artificial light in the middle would supply daylight. Bishop considered placing it at the Sun-Earth L4 and L5 points, stable spots along Earth's orbit 60 degrees ahead of and behind Earth, or closer to the Sun, or in the asteroid belt or beyond.

No one has tried to build it, and the idea has lived mainly in fiction. The rings in the Halo video games are close relatives. It tests the law at an extreme. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main agreement on space, does not forbid building new land, since Article II only stops countries claiming the Moon and other existing bodies and space itself. Article VIII says the country that registers an object launched into space keeps legal control over it and the people aboard. A ring the size of India would still be, on the wording of the treaty, one object under one country's flag, much as a ship is. Whether other countries would accept a country-sized habitat as an ordinary spacecraft is not known, because nothing of the kind has been tried. Its residents, like a ship's passengers, would have no independent state of their own unless other countries chose to recognise one.

edwards-sea-anchored-elevator.mechanism: Putting the base on the high seas, the ocean outside any country's control, avoids needing a host country. Under Articles VI, VII and VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the state responsible would still have to supervise it, would be liable for damage and would keep legal control of it.
edwards-sea-anchored-elevator.story:
A space elevator is a cable running from the ground far into space, held taut by a counterweight at its top as Earth turns, with climbing machines carrying cargo up and down it. The appeal is cost, since a climber does not have to carry its own fuel the way a rocket does. The idea had been around for decades, but experts expected it to take at least another 50 years because no known material was strong and light enough.

From 2000 the scientist Bradley Edwards proposed a way forward, a thin, wide ribbon of carbon nanotube composite, carbon nanotubes being an extremely strong material made of carbon atoms. A flat ribbon would also survive small meteor strikes better than a round cable. With support from NASA's Institute for Advanced Concepts, his work involved more than 20 institutions and 50 participants, and it covered how to put the ribbon up, how to power the climbers and how to avoid debris.

The base is the part that matters for territory. He suggested anchoring the ribbon in the western equatorial Pacific, where there is little lightning and few hurricanes, on a movable sea platform that could shift the ribbon out of the way of tracked space debris. Construction would begin with a seed cable of 19,800 kilograms, and 207 climbers would then add material until the ribbon reached about 750 tons and could lift 20 tons per climber.

Suppose such a platform were anchored on the high seas, the ocean beyond any country's control. It would need no host government's permission to occupy the spot, which could simplify negotiations over territory. It would not be free of law. A platform at sea would come under the country it was registered with, and under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the country responsible would have to authorise and supervise the activity. Under Article VII a launching country is liable for damage, and a falling ribbon could do a lot of it. The upper part of the cable would pass through the path of satellites of many countries. Philip Ragan, co-author of a book on space elevators, said the first country to deploy one could have a 95 percent cost advantage and potentially control all space activities. That gives other countries a strong reason to care who runs it.

The material has never been made at the strength and length required, and the elevator was never built.

kalpana-one.mechanism: Under Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the state that registers an object sent into space keeps legal control over it. Any such settlement would therefore live under that state's law.
kalpana-one.story:
Kalpana One is a design for a space settlement, a permanent home in space with far more living space than a space station. The design was revised in 2007 in a paper by Al Globus.

It is a short spinning cylinder with a radius of 250 metres and a length of 325 metres, built for 3,000 residents. People would live on the inside of the curved wall, and the spin would press them against it, feeling like gravity. Smaller cylinders inside would hold farms and recreation areas. Space radiation is the main danger to people living beyond Earth's protection, so the design calls for shielding of 10 metric tons per square metre, turning with the habitat. It belongs to a family of designs, among them Lewis One, also by Globus, and the McKendree cylinder of 1995, with a radius of 460 kilometres.

Location has become a live question for such designs. Designers once favoured the Moon's L4 and L5 points, stable spots 60 degrees ahead of and behind the Moon in its orbit. Those points are now thought too far from both Moon and Earth, and a settlement there would spend about two-thirds of its time outside the protection of Earth's magnetic field. A different orbit timed to the Moon, called a two-to-one resonance orbit, has been proposed.

No space settlement has been built. In law, a settlement of this kind would probably be treated as a large spacecraft. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty gives the state that registers an object legal control over it and over the people aboard, and Article VI requires that state to authorise and supervise private activities. So 3,000 residents would be living under the law of one country on Earth, which would decide matters such as crime, inheritance and taxes for them, unless that country agreed otherwise.

liftport.mechanism: A space elevator would need approval from whichever state controlled its base, but the company never got far enough for any state to have to decide. The only legal action it met concerned the sale of its shares.
liftport.story:
LiftPort Group is a private company in Washington state, founded in April 2003 by Michael Laine, that set out to build a space elevator. A space elevator is a cable running from the ground into space, with climbing machines carrying cargo along it, an idea that depends on carbon nanotubes, an extremely strong material made of carbon atoms.

The company's early years produced real tests on a small scale. On 12 November 2004 a climbing machine went up a ribbon about 90 metres tall at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in a snowstorm. On 20 September 2005 one climbed a 1,000-foot ribbon held up by a balloon. In January 2006 it held a platform on high-altitude balloons a mile up for more than six hours, while robots climbed more than 1,500 feet up a ribbon attached to it. That February it reported testing a mile of tether made of carbon fibre and fibreglass.

The grander plans did not arrive. On 29 April 2005 it announced a plant to make carbon nanotubes in Millville, New Jersey, due to open that June, and it set a goal of launching an elevator in 2010. The plant was never built. In 2007 the company faced a penalty over an alleged illegal offering of its shares, meaning it was said to have sold stock in the company outside the rules that protect investors. On 16 February 2010 it settled with the State of Washington, agreeing to stop specified activities, with no fine.

In October 2011 Laine turned to an elevator on the Moon as a first step, on the idea that the Moon's weaker gravity asks less of the material. A Kickstarter campaign in 2012 asked for $8,000 and raised $110,353 from 3,468 backers. Many have since asked in the comments what happened and received no reply. In April 2019 Laine admitted that little progress had been made despite more than $200,000 in seed funding.

No elevator has been built, so no government had to decide where one might go or who would control it. The only law the company actually met was ordinary company law on selling shares, the same rules that apply to any business on Earth.

obayashi-space-elevator.mechanism: An elevator is fixed to Earth at its base, so the country hosting the base, or the law of the high seas if it stands in open ocean, would set the terms before any space law applied.
obayashi-space-elevator.story:
This is a plan by Obayashi, a large Japanese construction company based in Tokyo, to build a space elevator, a cable running from the ground into space with climbing vehicles carrying cargo and people along it. In 2012 the company announced that it could build one by 2050 using carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms. A passenger vehicle would take 8 days to reach geosynchronous orbit, the height at which a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation. Obayashi published further details in 2016, and a report in 2018 described a small first test, with no outcome recorded.

The material is the main obstacle. A study by Feng Ding's team at Hong Kong Polytechnic University simulated a nanotube with a single atom out of place and found this cut its strength to 40 gigapascals, a unit of strength, when a cable would need about 50. Google X, Google's research division, began designing an elevator in 2014 and then put the project in what it called deep freeze after finding that no one had made a perfect strand longer than a metre. A 2019 study by the International Academy of Astronautics was more hopeful and judged an Earth elevator feasible.

The law would apply from the ground up. An elevator is fixed to Earth at its base, so a base on land would be under the country hosting it, which would set the terms, and a base in open ocean would come under the law of the high seas. Space law would take over only further up. A company of this kind would work with governments from the start and claim no new territory. Nothing has been built so far.

stanford-torus.mechanism: Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming the Moon and other bodies in space, but a colony in open space would stand on none of them. The rule that matters more here is Article VIII, which gives legal control to the state that registers the object.
stanford-torus.story:
The Stanford torus is a design for a wheel-shaped space colony, drawn up during a NASA summer study at Stanford University in California in 1975. Around 1970 the Princeton physicist Gerard O'Neill had set his students to calculate how large a space habitat could be, and the answers came back surprisingly large. That led NASA to sponsor summer workshops in the mid-1970s. The results appeared in 1977 as Space Settlements: A Design Study, by Richard Johnson and Charles Holbrow.

The design is a doughnut-shaped ring about 1.8 kilometres across, with a living tube 130 metres wide, for 10,000 permanent residents. It would turn once a minute, which would give people on the inner side of the outer ring between 0.9 and 1.0 of Earth's gravity. Standing inside would be like being in a long, narrow valley whose ends curve up and meet overhead. Six spokes with elevators would connect the ring to a central hub, where spacecraft would dock and where gravity is weakest. Mirrors would bring in sunlight through windows that make up a third of the tube's surface.

The ring's 5,600-metre circumference would be split into six sections, three for farms and three for housing, at about the density of a crowded suburb. Total mass would be about 10 million metric tons, and about 95 percent of that would be a shield against radiation, 1.7 metres of raw soil from the Moon. It would sit at the Earth-Moon L5 point, a stable spot in the Moon's orbit 60 degrees behind the Moon.

The economics were part of the plan. Residents would earn their keep building satellites to beam solar power to Earth, along with further colonies. That would give the settlement an export to pay its way.

Then there is the law. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main agreement on space, bars nations from claiming the Moon and other bodies in space. A colony in open space, built from Moon soil, would stand on none of them. The more relevant rule is Article VIII, which gives legal control over a spacecraft and its crew to the state that registers it. The 1975 study was a NASA project, so a colony built that way would presumably have been registered by the United States. It was never built, though a 2012 paper adapted the design for a generation ship, a ship meant to carry people for lifetimes.

artemis-project-europa.mechanism: Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty makes each state answer for its citizens' activities in space, so a private plan would need a state's authorisation and supervision. No such approval is recorded.
artemis-project-europa.story:
In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Europa, a moon of Jupiter whose surface is ice over a hidden ocean. It proposed igloos on the surface as bases for drilling through the ice to explore the water below, and it suggested people could live in air pockets inside the ice. That ocean may hold more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans, though metals and minerals would have to be brought in.

Radiation is the main barrier, because Jupiter's radiation belts cover Europa. An unshielded person would take about 5.40 sieverts a day, sieverts being a measure of radiation dose, when about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal. Heavy shielding might make a research base possible. The plan was never carried out.

The law asks something of even a private plan like this. Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty makes each state answer for its citizens' activities in space and requires authorisation and supervision, so the project would have needed a government's approval before leaving Earth. No such approval is recorded. Article II would have stopped any such government from claiming Europa on the settlers' behalf, and Article IX tells states to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds, a concern for an ocean that might hold life.

janhunen-ceres-megasatellite.mechanism: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space. Whether mining a body counts as claiming it is unsettled, and a settlement built from Ceres's material would depend on the answer.
janhunen-ceres-megasatellite.story:
This is a design for a large space settlement in high orbit around Ceres, the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. It was set out by Pekka Janhunen, a Finnish space physicist at the Finnish Meteorological Institute, in a preprint, a paper shared before formal publication, posted in November 2020 and revised in May 2021. He chose Ceres mainly for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires.

The settlers would not live on Ceres itself, where gravity is very weak. Spinning habitats would be attached by magnetic bearings to one huge disk-shaped frame in orbit, called a megasatellite, and the spin would give the same gravity as Earth. Mirrors would bring in sunlight. Because all the habitats share a frame, people could travel between them without using rocket fuel, and the settlement could keep growing past the living area of Earth. Population density would stay at 500 people per square kilometre, on soil 1.5 metres deep for gardens and trees, deepening to 4 metres if more energy were spent. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material, mostly soil and radiation shielding. The stated aim is a long-lasting world in which all atoms are recycled. A space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply, which the author considers feasible because of the low gravity and fast rotation.

The legal problem is what the settlement is made from. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space, but it does not say clearly whether digging up and keeping their material counts as claiming them. Some countries have passed laws saying their companies may keep what they extract, and others argue this breaks the treaty. A settlement built entirely of Ceres would depend on the answer. Once built, it would be a spacecraft in orbit under the state that registered it. It remains a paper design.

nasa-hope-callisto.mechanism: Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming a moon as their own. A state base would be legal only as long as it did not amount to such a claim.
nasa-hope-callisto.story:
HOPE, short for Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration, was a NASA study in 2003 of how people might reach the outer planets. It chose Callisto, a moon of Jupiter, because Callisto orbits outside Jupiter's radiation belt, the zone of harmful radiation that surrounds the planet and makes closer moons such as Europa and Io far more dangerous. A base on the surface could make fuel for further exploration of the solar system. Callisto has accessible water, silicate rock and metals, gravity of about 0.13 of Earth's, and probably an ocean inside it.

A crew's round trip was estimated at about 2 to 5 years, assuming major advances in propulsion. The work stopped at the study stage, and no mission followed.

Because NASA is a government agency, the legal questions would have been simple compared with a private venture. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming a moon as their own, and Article VIII would keep the base and crew under US authority. Article XII says stations on other worlds are to be open to visits from other treaty members, on a mutual basis and with notice. So a base would be American property on ground that nobody owns.

titan-settlement-proposals.mechanism: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space. States disagree over whether extracting resources counts as claiming, so any plan built on Titan's hydrocarbons would face that open question.
titan-settlement-proposals.story:
Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, has been proposed as a site for human settlement, more seriously than most places that far from Earth. It has a thick atmosphere of nitrogen and methane, and it is the only known world besides Earth with lakes on its surface, though these hold liquid methane and ethane in place of water, and range from about 1 to 100 kilometres across.

The main advocate is Robert Zubrin, an American aerospace engineer and founder of the Mars Society. In his 1999 book Entering Space he wrote that Saturn is the most valuable of the giant planets, because it is relatively close, has low radiation and has a good system of moons, and that Titan is the best moon for a base. He has called it in certain ways the most hospitable world beyond Earth for colonisation. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as a home for life in the magazine Analog in 1992.

The supplies are the attraction. Nitrogen could fill out breathing air, as it does on Earth. Water thought to lie beneath the surface could yield oxygen. Nitrogen, methane and ammonia could make fertiliser. Radar studies published in 2008 by Ralph Lorenz's team found hundreds of times more hydrocarbons than Earth's known oil and gas reserves. Power could come from nuclear plants, or from turbines in methane seas where Saturn's pull causes tides of up to a metre. The thick air and weak gravity mean a person in a suit could strap on wings and fly.

The objections are serious. Titan is extremely cold. There is no free oxygen, so burning fuel as on Earth does not work. Gravity is about one-seventh of Earth's, and the long-term effects on bone and muscle, and on children growing up there, are unknown, since all research has been in zero gravity. Children raised there might not be able to adjust to Earth.

No one has gone past proposals on paper. The law would be tested if they did. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space, so no settlement could own Titan. States disagree over whether extracting resources counts as claiming, so any plan built on Titan's hydrocarbons would face that open question. Settlers would also remain under the law of whichever country registered their craft and base, however long a message took to reach them.

abalonia-cortes-bank.mechanism: A coastal state has exclusive rights over the resources of its continental shelf, the shallow seabed off its coast. The US used that rule against later plans for this bank, and the same rule stopped similar projects off Florida.
abalonia-cortes-bank.story:
Abalonia was a planned country on Cortes Bank, a shallow undersea mountain range in the Pacific about 111 miles west of San Diego, California, and the outermost feature of California's Channel Islands chain. It was an island about 10,000 years ago, when sea levels were lower. Today its highest point, Bishop Rock, lies just under the surface, and giant waves break there, which later made it famous among surfers.

In 1966 a team of entrepreneurs including Jim Houtz planned to turn the bank into a constitutional monarchy. They reasoned that because the bank lay in international waters, beyond any country's coast, maritime law would let them rule their own nation. A newspaper first reported the plan on 31 October 1966, under the headline "Pair Planning Island Nation off San Diego". A pro golfer and film actor, Joe Kirkwood Jr., wrote a 60-page account of the affair around 1967 that was never published. The business plan was food. They would sink a concrete-hulled Second World War freighter, the SS Jalisco, on Bishop Rock, surround it with a growing ring of boulders, and use it as a seafood processing plant.

The ship was towed out from San Francisco, passing under the Bay Bridge. Waves broke it apart on the rock and the crew were nearly killed. Houtz, who was aboard and was injured, later told the writer Chris Dixon that the affair cost him his marriage and left him in financial ruin. The wreck lies in three pieces in 6 to 40 feet of water, and divers visit it.

The legal theory did not survive long either. When another company later proposed a nation called Taluga on the same bank, the US government declared it US territory as part of the continental shelf, the shallow seabed extending from a country's coast. A coastal state holds exclusive rights to the resources of its shelf, so a platform there could expect to meet US law even if the water above it was open sea. The same reasoning stopped similar projects off Florida in the same years. No state had to act against Abalonia itself, because the waves had already destroyed the ship.

autopia-saya-de-malha.mechanism: Open ocean belongs to no state, so the founders expected no legal obstacle on a mid-ocean bank. Any part of the bank within 200 miles of a state's coast falls in that state's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources.
autopia-saya-de-malha.story:
Autopia was a planned micronation, a small self-declared state, on the Saya de Malha Bank, one of the largest underwater plateaus in the world, northeast of Madagascar and southeast of the Seychelles. The bank covers about 40,800 square kilometres, roughly the size of Belgium by its promoters' description. Parts of it are less than 33 feet deep and covered with sea grass and small coral reefs. The nearest land, tiny Agaléga, is about 300 kilometres away.

The people behind it were the architect Wolf Hilbertz, a professor at the University of Houston, and the marine biologist Thomas Goreau. Hilbertz had patented Biorock, a process that passes a weak electric current through steel frames sunk in seawater, which slowly deposits limestone on them. It creates a surface where corals and shellfish can grow. He hoped to grow buildings this way, with less carbon cost than ordinary concrete, and to create a self-sufficient settlement "that belongs to the residents who live and work there". The name meant the place that builds itself.

The legal attraction was the location. In 2004 Hilbertz said most of the bank lay in international waters, on the high seas, the ocean outside any country's control, governed only by the UN Law of the Sea. The reporter Ian Urbina describes it as hundreds of miles beyond any nation's reach. Wikipedia says that Mauritius administers the whole bank, because part of it lies in Mauritius's exclusive economic zone, the 200-mile belt in which a coastal state controls resources, and that most of the bank is otherwise in international waters. So a builder on the bank might face a claim from Mauritius, depending on the exact spot. Even in open water, the Law of the Sea does not let anyone claim the seabed as a country.

On 9 March 1997 the two men sailed three days from Victoria in the Seychelles with solar panels, metal scaffolding and cornerstones. In 2002 they returned in three sailboats with architects, cartographers and marine biologists from several countries. With a cyclone approaching, they built a steel frame five by five metres and two metres high in six days, at 9°12′ south, anchored to the seabed and kept charged by a small battery. Nobody settled there. The plans then stalled for lack of money, so the question of who governed the site was never tested.

The bank later drew another plan. The Italian businessman Samuele Landi, who had been convicted of fraud in Italy and was sentenced in his absence to 14 years, planned to bring barges there from Dubai, far from the reach of extradition. He lived for over a year on a barge called Aisland anchored off Dubai while raising money. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke the barge in two, and Landi and two crew members died, so that plan never reached the bank.

grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.mechanism: United States v. Ray (1970) held that a coastal state can stop building on its continental shelf, the seabed off its coast, without owning that seabed. Its exclusive rights to the resources there are enough for a court to order the work stopped.
grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.story:
Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold were two rival plans to found new countries on Triumph and Long Reefs, two coral reefs about four and a half miles off southeast Florida near Miami. The reefs are underwater except for brief exposure at low tide. In the early 1960s the United States claimed only a narrow belt of sea as its own, and these reefs lay beyond it, so the promoters believed no state could stop them building. A court later called them reefs underlying the high seas.

Louis M. Ray and his firm, Acme General Contractors, planned Grand Capri, a resort island. They placed caissons, large watertight boxes, on the reefs and filled them with material dredged from the seabed. A rival, Atlantis Development Corporation, said an earlier discovery gave it better title and planned commercial buildings on pilings. So there were two private parties arguing about who owned something that, at high tide, could not be seen.

The first official contact was a building permit. On 16 November 1964 Acme applied to the US Army Corps of Engineers, the federal agency that regulates building in waterways, to build a 20-acre resort island. The application itself suggested that Acme expected US rules to matter. The Corps refused, and Ray dredged anyway.

The government went to court. A trial court in southern Florida ordered a temporary halt in April 1965. In January 1969 it barred construction but rejected the government's trespass claim, because the government did not own the reefs. That raised the key question. Trespass means entering someone else's property, and the United States did not own the reefs, so it needed some other legal ground for stopping a builder.

The government appealed. In 1970 the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit answered that question in United States v. Ray. It held that the reefs were part of the outer continental shelf, the seabed extending from the coast. US law and the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf give the United States exclusive rights there to explore and exploit resources. The court ordered a full permanent ban on construction, noting harm to corals and to shipping.

The rule matters to anyone planning a territory on a reef. A coastal country does not need to own the seabed or claim the water above it. Its exclusive right to the resources is enough to let a court stop the work. Shallow reefs near a coast are the most tempting sites for building, and they are the very places this rule covers. Nobody ever lived on either project, and both ended in the courtroom.

minerva.mechanism: Land built by hand on a reef does not become a state just because no one has yet claimed the reef. Here nearby states responded by agreeing that one of them should annex it, meaning formally add it to its territory.
minerva.story:
The Republic of Minerva was an attempt in 1972 to create a new country on the Minerva Reefs, two ring-shaped coral reefs in the South Pacific between Fiji and Tonga, about 270 miles west of Tonga's capital. They were named after the whaling ship Minerva, wrecked there in 1829. The reef surface stands about three feet out of the water at low tide and about four feet under at high tide, so it was a hazard to ships and nobody lived on it.

Its backer was Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer and coin dealer, and a concentration camp survivor. In 1968 he published A New Constitution for a New Country, a model for a state with very limited government paid for voluntarily. He wanted a country with no taxation, welfare, subsidies or economic intervention, where people could do as they pleased if they did not infringe on others' rights. Income would come from fees paid by banks and multinational companies that based themselves there.

He raised money from about 2,000 investors through a body called the Ocean Life Research Foundation, with offices in New York and London. He first tried to buy an island from a government, and no one would sell sovereignty, so the group chose to build its own land. Accounts of the construction differ. Some say barges or a dredging ship brought sand from Australia, while another describes a small party sailing from Fiji in January 1971 with coral wrapped in chicken wire, concrete blocks and rubble. The result was two tiny islands with a stone platform and a flag, a torch on a blue background. The plan was for a resort called Sea City with 30,000 people. No one actually lived there. Minerva dollar coins were struck, including a 35-dollar piece.

A declaration of independence went to neighbouring states and about a hundred nations on 19 January 1972. Morris "Bud" Davis was named provisional president and ran the republic from his living room in Gustine, California.

Neighbours reacted because of what it might mean for them. Tonga had not included the reefs in its 1887 territorial claim, and Fiji's prime minister asked what would stop such people claiming land in Fiji. Australia also objected to a private state in its region. At a conference on 24 February, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles as its own on 15 June. An expedition arrived on 18 June. On 21 June the king, Taufaʻahau Tupou IV, sailed out on the royal yacht with soldiers, a convict work party and a four-piece brass band. He tore down the flag and read a proclamation of sovereignty, and the platform was dismantled within hours. In one account a fight between two of the convicts left one of them dead. In September the South Pacific Forum named Tonga as the only possible owner, without explicitly recognising its title.

Oliver then dismissed Davis and the project collapsed. He went on to back separatists on Abaco in the Bahamas and on Vanuatu, where troops from Australia and Papua New Guinea crushed the revolt.

The case shows the weakness of the empty-reef idea. International law makes land that no state holds open to the first state that takes it, and a private person is not a state. Once an unclaimed reef became a problem, a neighbour could simply claim it, and the region agreed. A sand pile with no population, army or recognition had nothing to set against that.

minerva-1982-and-fiji-tonga.mechanism: Force ended the private claim, but annexing the reef left two states arguing over what sea rights it creates. Under the law of the sea, a recognised feature can give its owner rights over the waters around it.
minerva-1982-and-fiji-tonga.story:
The Minerva Reefs are two submerged atolls, or ring-shaped coral reefs, between Fiji and Tonga in the South Pacific. Tonga annexed them in 1972 to stop a private group founding a libertarian country there. The sequel has two parts, one small and private, the other between two states.

In 1982 a group of Americans led by Morris "Bud" Davis, the former provisional president of that Republic of Minerva, tried to occupy the reefs again. By then Tonga had held them for a decade and had raised its flag there. Tongan troops forced the group off after three weeks. No later group is reported to have taken possession, and Reason magazine later described the structure as more or less reclaimed by the sea. A second attempt had no better legal footing than the first and now faced a state in possession.

The argument then passed to the two neighbours, for a reason that has little to do with living there. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the 1982 treaty on states' rights at sea, a feature can be used in measuring how much surrounding ocean a country controls, including its fish and seabed minerals. So a reef that seems useless can be worth a great deal of water. In 2005 Fiji declared that it did not recognise any maritime claims by Tonga based on the reefs. That November Fiji complained to the International Seabed Authority, the body that oversees the deep ocean floor, and Tonga lodged a counter-claim.

The two countries then acted out the dispute at sea. In 2010 Fiji's navy destroyed navigation lights at the entrance to the lagoon, and in late May 2011 it again destroyed navigation equipment Tonga had installed. In early June 2011 two Tongan navy ships went to replace it. Such lights matter because a state that maintains things on a reef is showing that it runs the place. In July 2014 Tonga's lands minister proposed giving the reefs to Fiji in exchange for the Lau Islands. The dispute is not known to have been settled.

new-atlantis.mechanism: The 1856 Guano Islands Act lets US citizens claim islands with guano deposits for the United States. Hemingway stretched it to cover a man-made raft, and no court tested the idea because storms destroyed the raft first.
new-atlantis.story:
New Atlantis was a tiny republic on a raft off Jamaica, created by Leicester Hemingway, the younger brother of the novelist Ernest Hemingway. Les Hemingway was a writer and sailor who had spent years around the Bahamas and Miami and whose 1962 biography of his brother gave him some money. His stated goals were to experiment with democracy and to study marine life.

He built the raft of bamboo, steel, iron pipe and rock, 8 by 30 feet, had it towed about 6 to 8 miles off Bluefields, Jamaica, onto a shallow bank in waters then considered international, and anchored it with an old Ford engine block. On 4 July 1964 he declared a republic, though one profile gives 1965. He typed a constitution copied almost word for word from that of the United States.

His legal claim was inventive. The US Guano Islands Act of 1856 lets American citizens claim islands with deposits of guano, seabird droppings then valued as fertiliser, on behalf of the United States, provided the islands belong to no other government. Hemingway argued that his raft was technically an island. He gave the half of the raft where birds were encouraged to leave droppings to the United States and kept the rest as his nation. His daughter's profile says there was no guano on the raft until he brought it himself.

By 1965 six people were listed as inhabitants: Hemingway, his wife Doris, their daughters Anne, 7, and Hilary, 3, and a public relations man and his assistant. They unanimously elected him president, and it made front-page news in Jamaica. In practice the family lived in Miami, and the press release named Coconut Grove as the capital. Doris sewed a flag. The currency was the scruple, made up of items such as fish hooks, carob beans and shark teeth. His daughters recall him selling citizenships and titles in Miami bars in exchange for investment.

He also claimed the seafloor 50 feet below and planned to pile up rocks into an island. He formed the International Marine Research Society, and wanted to pay for its work by selling stamps, but the Universal Postal Union, the international body that coordinates mail, refused them. He mailed a stamp showing Lyndon Johnson to the White House, and a State Department letter addressed to the "Acting President" was presented as recognition. A letter's polite form of address does not amount to diplomatic recognition, which requires a government's deliberate decision.

Within a few years tropical storms destroyed the raft, and local fishermen salvaged the wreckage. One account has the first storm taking it within a year. A raft is also a weak basis for a claim, since the law of the sea treats an island as naturally formed land, and no court tested the idea. Hemingway died in 1982. The flag and other papers went to the Harry Ransom Center in Texas in 1966.

new-utopia.mechanism: US securities law, which governs the sale of investments, applied to internet sales aimed at US investors whatever flag or territory the offer claimed. Promising a future sovereign country gave no protection from fraud rules.
new-utopia.story:
New Utopia was a planned tax-free country on concrete platforms over the Misteriosa Bank, an underwater rise in the Caribbean about 115 miles west of the Cayman Islands. It was never built and existed only as an offer to investors, which is how US law reached it.

Howard Turney, who lived in Houston and Tulsa, had become an advocate of human growth hormone and in 1993 opened an anti-ageing clinic in Mexico. Around 1995 he renamed himself Lazarus Long after a long-lived character in Robert Heinlein's novels, called himself Prince Lazarus, and filed a claim to the bank with the United Nations. A UN office has no power to approve such a claim.

The plan drew on Ayn Rand and Heinlein. There would be no income tax, with services paid for by a 20 percent tax on imported consumer goods. Plans included 642 apartments, a casino like Monte Carlo's, and a clinic better than the Mayo Clinic. A website of more than 100 pages drew over 100,000 visits. It offered five-year government bonds, meaning loans to the new country, at 9.5 percent interest, in a $350 million offering, and invited buyers to become charter citizens. It also promised currency returns as high as 200 percent, and showed notes with Long's face.

This is where his location mattered less than his customers. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which polices the sale of investments, treats an offer aimed at American investors as subject to US law, wherever the supposed project lies. On 8 April 1999 the SEC filed suit, alleging false statements about construction, the companies involved, the safety of the investment and the SEC's own inquiry. An SEC official said people were making investment decisions based on what they read on a website. Judge Michael Burrage in Tulsa, Oklahoma, issued an emergency order freezing the money, which the Associated Press put near $100,000 at that stage. Long called it a witch-hunt, said he would return the money, and said he wanted people to be able to keep donating to the New Utopia government.

On 20 January 2000 Long accepted a final judgment without contesting it and was barred from further violations. The SEC waived repayment of $24,000 plus interest because he swore he could not pay. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised, while encyclopedia entries claim $100 million.

Long died in April 2012. His daughter, Elizabeth Henderson, announced a revival in 2017, promising completion by 2021, and nothing is known to have come of it. For anyone founding a territory, the case shows that a future country has no shield. Selling bonds in a state that does not exist is a sale of investments by a person who lives somewhere, to buyers who live somewhere, and those places' laws apply.

operation-atlantis.mechanism: A shallow reef that two nearby states both claim offers no empty legal space. A coastal navy could remove an unarmed group without any court being involved.
operation-atlantis.story:
Operation Atlantis was an effort to found a new country in the Caribbean, begun in 1968 by Werner Stiefel. Born in Brooklyn in 1921, Stiefel ran the family's Stiefel Medicinal Soap Company, which became the largest privately owned skin-care drug firm in the world. He was inspired by the writer Ayn Rand, especially her novel Atlas Shrugged, and believed postwar America was heading to socialism. He wanted, in his words, to test whether a free capitalist society could exist and flourish.

He set out a plan in three stages. Atlantis I was a motel in Saugerties, New York, near one of his soap plants, where followers would gather and work. Atlantis II was a ship that would sail under the new country's flag in international waters. Atlantis III would be a ship plus an island, a sovereign country as close to US shores as possible. He wrote a book under the pen name Warren K. Stevens to recruit people, and published a monthly bulletin. He paid Spencer Heath MacCallum with a 2 percent share to draft a constitution. Members struck a coin, the deca, holding a decagram of silver, on a soap press. Stiefel kept the project out of the press, so many details are hard to confirm, and how many lived at the motel is not known.

His first choice of land was the Prickly Pear Cays near Anguilla in 1969. He agreed to pay $100,000 and the sale fell through, and one account says the Anguillan government declined to sell.

So he decided to make land. Members spent a year building a 38-foot concrete boat, Atlantis II, under a geodesic dome beside the motel. Launched on the Hudson River in December 1971 at high tide, it capsized as the tide fell and lay sideways in the mud. It was righted, and sailed south, broke a propeller shaft and reached the Bahamas, where a storm destroyed it.

Stiefel bought another ship and went to Silver Shoals, a reef area with water four feet deep at low tide, thought to hold Spanish shipwrecks, and claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas. He built sea walls and was about to dredge up sand when gunboats ordered the group to leave. Accounts differ on whether they were Haitian or Dominican. One says the captain took them for pirates diving on wrecks. The group was unarmed, and Stiefel, described as appalled by violence, left. He then leased a base on Tortuga, a Haitian island, until officials read the group's newsletter and cancelled the lease. That is a recurring problem for such ventures. Publicity needed to recruit followers also tells the local government what they plan.

An oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank between Honduras and Cuba was destroyed by a hurricane, and most members went home. A participant says the group later bought a six-acre island, Hatchet Caye in Belize, and lived there until 2005. There Stiefel sought freeport status from the Belizean government, and in Belize they were ordinary landowners under Belizean law.

The five years show the order in which the obstacles appear. Nobody will sell sovereignty. Built land in shallow water sits in someone's claimed area. A small navy can remove an unarmed group with no court involved. What a private buyer can actually get is an ordinary island in an ordinary country.

condominiums-new-hebrides-andorra-brcko.mechanism: Two or more states can agree to govern a territory together, an arrangement known as a condominium. Such shared rule can last for decades and can lead to independence, as it did for Vanuatu and Nauru.
condominiums-new-hebrides-andorra-brcko.story:
A condominium, in international law, is a territory shared and governed by two or more powers at once. The word is the same as for a block of flats, and the idea is similar, with several owners holding one property. It is a way of settling a quarrel when neither side will give up its claim, and it has produced some odd daily arrangements.

New Hebrides, a chain of islands in the South Pacific, was a French and British condominium from 1906 until it became independent in 1980 as the republic now called Vanuatu. Nauru, also in the Pacific, was run jointly by Australia, New Zealand and Britain until independence in 1968. Others have been the Oregon Country in North America, shared by Britain and the United States from 1818 to 1846, and the Samoan Islands from 1889 to 1899.

Brčko District in Bosnia and Herzegovina shows the idea at work today, inside one country. Bosnia has two internal entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, and neither would give the town up after the war of the 1990s. The district, created on 8 March 2000, is held jointly by both because of its mixed population. It has 493 square kilometres and 83,516 people.

Andorra, in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, is a different case that often gets mixed in. French law once treated it as a French and Spanish condominium. It is itself a sovereign state, and it is more commonly called a co-principality, because two foreigners share its head of state by virtue of their offices, the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain.

All these arrangements came from agreements between the powers concerned. For a founder the lesson is about where a shared status comes from. A private group cannot declare one, because only the states holding the claim can agree to it. Two of these territories later became independent, which shows that shared rule can also be a stage on the way to a new state. Brčko remains a shared district.

corpus-separatum-jerusalem.mechanism: A General Assembly plan is a recommendation and takes effect only if the parties on the ground accept it or someone enforces it. Here no one did, so the international city never existed.
corpus-separatum-jerusalem.story:
Corpus separatum, Latin for "separated body", was a United Nations plan to place Jerusalem and its surroundings under international government, belonging to neither of the two states proposed around it. It is an example of a territory designed on paper to be outside every country.

The background was the end of British rule over Palestine, which Britain had governed since the First World War. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181, the Partition Plan, which proposed separate Arab and Jewish states. Jerusalem was to have special status because of its importance to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and the idea drew on the Vatican's long concern for the Christian holy places.

The area ran from Abu Dis in the east to Bethlehem in the south, Ein Karim in the west and Shuʻfat in the north. A governor appointed by the UN Trusteeship Council, the UN body overseeing territories not yet self-governing, would run it under a statute written by that council. All residents would automatically become citizens of the City of Jerusalem unless they chose citizenship of the Arab or Jewish state. The statute would be reviewed after ten years, with the citizens taking part through a referendum. So it had the features of a small state, with citizens, a head of government and a founding law.

It was never carried out. Palestinian and other Arab leaders first rejected the partition, though Arab governments later supported the international plan. The British took no steps to set up the regime and left on 14 May 1948. In the war that followed, the fighting in Jerusalem ended on 18 July 1948 with Israel holding the west of the city and Transjordan, now Jordan, the east. In December 1948 the General Assembly's Resolution 194 set up a commission to work out a permanent international regime with as much local autonomy as possible. In December 1949 Israeli prime minister David Ben-Gurion declared the plan void, and the General Assembly reaffirmed it days later, but the statute approved in 1950 was never applied. Israel by then favoured at most a limited regime for the holy places.

A General Assembly resolution is a recommendation, and the UN has no government of its own to put one into effect. Someone on the ground has to accept it or enforce it, and the forces on the ground were fighting for the city. In 2012 the European Parliament and the General Assembly expressed support for Jerusalem as a dual capital of Israel and a State of Palestine, and the city's status remains disputed. What the case shows is that even the world's main international body cannot create a territory by voting for one.

eastern-slavonia-untaes.mechanism: The UN can run disputed land directly for a fixed period, with the aim of returning it to the state that claims it. The parties' own agreement gave the UN that role here.
eastern-slavonia-untaes.story:
Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium is a region along the Danube River in eastern Croatia that was run directly by the United Nations for two years, so it could return to Croatia without more fighting. When Yugoslavia broke up in the early 1990s, Croatia fought a war of independence, and local Serbs held this region after battles at places such as Vukovar. By late 1995 Croatia had retaken other Serb-held areas by force, in Operation Storm, and this was the last one left.

The Erdut Agreement of November 1995, between the Croatian government and the local Serb representatives, set up a peaceful transition and invited the UN in. UN Security Council Resolution 1037 then created the UN Transitional Authority, known as UNTAES, on 15 January 1996. It was only the third UN mission in history, after Western New Guinea and Cambodia, with direct power to govern. At full strength it had about 4,800 soldiers, 99 military observers and 400 police. The American diplomat Jacques Paul Klein led it first, followed by William Walker.

The daily work involved small, practical problems. The UN had to see the region demilitarised, and it had to rebuild a police force in a place where the police had been part of the first ethnic clashes. Serb officers wore Yugoslav symbols and would not give them up, so UNTAES bought uniforms with no national insignia at all, using money from the US Department of Justice. Croatia at first refused to pay the local police, then agreed, since paying them showed that Croatian authority was returning. Croatia would not pay in Yugoslav dinars and the officers would not take Croatian kuna, so they were paid in German marks. Top police posts each had two holders, one Croat and one Serb. The UN also helped Serbs missing Croatian documents to obtain them so they could vote, and organised voting for Croatia's Chamber of Counties, the upper house of parliament, on 13 April 1997.

The mission ended on 15 January 1998, and the UN says it peacefully reintegrated the territory into Croatia. A smaller UN police support group followed for a time. The region remains part of Croatia.

This was the opposite of a founding. The UN governed the land while never treating it as anything but Croatian, with the aim of giving it back. It shows that being under international rule does not place a territory outside every country. The UN's power there came from the parties' own agreement and the Security Council, and it lasted exactly as long as those allowed.

free-city-of-danzig.mechanism: A city-state protected by an international body depends on that body being willing and able to defend it. The League of Nations guarantee did not stop Germany annexing Danzig in 1939.
free-city-of-danzig.story:
The Free City of Danzig was a small self-governing state on the Baltic coast, centred on the port now called Gdańsk in Poland. It existed from 1920 to 1939, and it is the classic case of a city made independent by treaty under an international guarantee.

It came out of a dilemma at the end of the First World War. US President Woodrow Wilson's peace plan promised newly independent Poland secure access to the sea, which suggested giving it the port. About 90 percent of Danzig's people were German, though, and handing them to Poland would have broken the principle of letting peoples decide their own rule. The Allies compromised in Article 100 of the 1919 Treaty of Versailles, by taking the city from Germany without giving it to Poland.

The city and nearly 200 smaller places became a city-state of 1,952 square kilometres, with 366,730 people in 1923, set up on 15 November 1920. It stood under the direct protection of the League of Nations, the international body of the time, whose High Commissioner lived there and oversaw it. It had its own parliament, the Volkstag, a government called the Senate, a police force, passports and from 1923 its own currency, the gulden. It was not fully independent, because Poland handled its foreign relations and defence, shared a customs union with it and ran its railways and post, and had rights at the port. The population was mostly Protestant and Catholic, with a small Jewish community, and a Polish minority whose party received about 3 to 6 percent of the vote.

Those shared powers caused constant quarrels, since Danzig's people wanted to be German and Poland relied on the port. To reduce its dependence, Poland began building a rival port at Gdynia in 1921, and by 1933 Gdynia's trade had passed Danzig's. The Nazi Party won about 50 percent of the Volkstag vote on 28 May 1933 and took over the Senate that June, and by 1936 it had a majority. Local Nazis pressed to rejoin Germany. The League's High Commissioner could report on this, but the League had no force of its own to stop it.

On 1 September 1939 Germany attacked Poland, firing on the Polish depot at Westerplatte in Danzig harbour, and the Free City was annexed. Local forces fought alongside German troops at the Polish post office. The Nazis persecuted the Poles and Jews who lived there, sending many to the nearby Stutthof camp. Soviet and Polish troops took the city in 1945, it went to Poland, and most of its German residents were expelled or left.

For anyone designing a territory outside existing states, Danzig offers a real example and a warning. A treaty really can create a separate state with a parliament, money and passports, and it lasted nearly 19 years. Its survival depended on its guarantor being able and willing to defend it, and on its neighbours accepting the arrangement, which Germany never did.

free-territory-of-trieste.mechanism: A state created on paper by treaty and the UN cannot function if the officials it requires are never appointed. Trieste's governor never was, so the two occupying powers kept running it until they divided it.
free-territory-of-trieste.story:
The Free Territory of Trieste was meant to be a neutral independent country on the Adriatic Sea between Italy and Yugoslavia, under the direct responsibility of the UN Security Council. It existed in law for seven years and was never run as a country.

Trieste is a port with a mixed Italian and Slovene population and it mattered for trade with Central Europe. At the end of the Second World War, Yugoslav troops took the city, and on 10 June 1945 an agreement at Duino set a dividing line, the Morgan Line, after which they withdrew to their own side. Both Italy and Yugoslavia wanted the port. The planned solution was to give it to neither. In January 1947 Security Council Resolution 16 called for a free state, and the Treaty of Peace with Italy of 10 February 1947 created it, taking effect on 15 September 1947. Its official languages would be Italian and Slovene.

Everything hinged on one post. Its permanent statute would take effect once an international governor was appointed with the approval of the four main powers. The Cold War stopped that. Between October 1947 and March 1948 the Soviet Union rejected 12 successive candidates, and on 20 March 1948 the United States, Britain and France recommended returning the territory to Italy. So no governor was ever appointed, no local government was formed, and its status went on being generally respected only in form.

Instead it stayed split in two along the old line. Zone A, the city and coast, had 222.5 square kilometres and 262,406 people under British and American military rule. Zone B, with 515.5 square kilometres and 71,000 people, was under the Yugoslav army. Each used its own version of the lira, and there were separate postage stamps. For seven years the people of Trieste lived under military governors. The territory still sent a cycling team to a race in Poland in 1950.

On 5 October 1954 the United States, Britain, Italy and Yugoslavia signed the London Memorandum, which ended Allied rule in Zone A. Italy took Zone A and Yugoslavia kept Zone B. The Treaty of Osimo, signed in 1975 and in force from 1977, settled the border between them, so the territory no longer exists. The case shows how much depends on the great powers still agreeing after they have signed. A treaty and a Security Council resolution created this state, and a single unfilled post left it without a government.

memel-klaipeda.mechanism: A treaty can take land from one state without settling who gets it next. Here that left it open to seizure by a neighbour, whose title the Allies then accepted, and later to loss under threat from a stronger state.
memel-klaipeda.story:
The Memel Territory, now the Klaipėda Region of Lithuania, was a strip of 2,657 square kilometres on the Baltic coast, with the port of Memel, or Klaipėda, at its north end. Between the world wars it passed through several hands, and for a time it belonged to no state in the normal sense.

It had been part of Germany's East Prussia. Under Article 99 of the 1919 Treaty of Versailles, Germany gave it up in favour of the victorious Allies, who said its port was the only sea outlet for newly independent Lithuania. They did not hand it over, though. Most people there spoke German, and Prussian Lithuanians made up about 26.6 percent, and many of those did not want to join Lithuania either. So it was left in suspense, run for the Allies under the Conference of Ambassadors, a committee of their diplomats.

The French general Dominique Odry took charge in February 1920, and High Commissioner Gabriel Petisné followed in May 1921, with French troops present. In this waiting period the idea of an independent Memelland grew. A local group, the German-Lithuanian homeland federation, had 30,000 members, about 21 percent of the population, and wanted a free state that might later rejoin Germany. Emergency banknotes and overprinted French stamps served as its money and post.

In January 1923 Lithuanian militias, mainly from Lithuania itself, staged the Klaipėda Revolt and occupied the territory. France was busy occupying the Ruhr in Germany at the same time, and its garrison did little to stop them. On 19 January Lithuania annexed the region. The Allies accepted what had happened. A convention of 8 May 1924 confirmed the annexation and gave the region wide self-rule, with its own parliament, two official languages, taxes, courts and even separate citizenship. A Lithuanian census in 1925 counted 141,000 people, with German the largest language group.

By late 1938 Lithuania had lost control of local politics. On 23 March 1939, after an oral German ultimatum, Lithuania's foreign minister Juozas Urbšys and his German counterpart Joachim von Ribbentrop signed a treaty handing the territory to Germany. Hitler sailed in on a warship at dawn. Britain and France did nothing. After 1945 the Soviet Union made it part of Soviet Lithuania, and most remaining Germans were expelled or later left. It stayed part of Lithuania when the country regained independence in 1990.

Local support for a free state counted for little in any of this. The case shows that land detached from one state with no clear next owner invites whoever is nearest and strongest. The international committee meant to hold it did not defend it, and then accepted the result.

saar-basin-1920-1935.mechanism: A treaty can suspend a state's government over land for a fixed term and hand the final choice to the residents. The Saar's 1935 vote carried that out, returning it to Germany.
saar-basin-1920-1935.story:
The Territory of the Saar Basin was a coal-mining region on the border of Germany and France, centred on Saarbrücken, taken out of German government for 15 years by the 1919 Treaty of Versailles. For that time it was governed by an international body and belonged, in practice, to no country.

The reason was coal and compensation. During the First World War, mines in northern France had been destroyed. Under Article 45 of the treaty Germany gave the Saar's coal mines to France as compensation. Under Article 49 Germany gave up governing the territory in favour of the League of Nations, the international body of the time, which held it as a trustee. The treaty delayed the final decision, with residents to vote on their future after 15 years.

A five-member Governing Commission ruled from 1920 and alone made the law. It had to include at least one French person and one German resident of the Saar, and its chairmen came from France, Canada and Britain. A 30-member regional council formed in 1922 could only advise, so the 812,000 people living there in 1933 had little say in their own government. The territory had the Saar franc, its own postage stamps and, in the mines, a French employer. The great majority were German, and the arrangement was unpopular.

Then came Hitler. After 1933 the Saar was the only part of Germany still under foreign rule, so opponents of the Nazis fled there, and anti-Nazi groups campaigned to keep the League's rule. Joseph Goebbels ran a large campaign for return, and local Catholic leaders also supported it. In the vote of 13 January 1935, on a 98 percent turnout, 90.8 percent chose to rejoin Germany, 8.8 percent to keep the existing status and 0.4 percent to join France. Refugees who could not stay were later resettled, some of them in Paraguay.

The territory ended on 1 March 1935 and returned to Germany. After the Second World War the Saar was again separated, as a French-controlled protectorate from 1947 to 1956. A referendum on 23 October 1955 ended French rule, and the Saarland joined West Germany on 1 January 1957. It remains a German state.

The case is one of the few where the plan worked exactly as written. A treaty suspended a state's rule, an international body governed, and the residents chose at the agreed time. It also shows that a temporary international status does not create a new people or state, because when asked, nearly everyone wanted to go back.

tangier-international-zone.mechanism: Foreign states can run a territory jointly by agreement among themselves, without making it their own. The arrangement ended when the local state regained full independence and took the territory back by agreement.
tangier-international-zone.story:
The Tangier International Zone was an area of 373 square kilometres around the Moroccan port of Tangier, on the Strait of Gibraltar, run jointly by foreign powers for about three decades. It is among the longest-lived examples of a territory governed by no single state, and it became known as an offshore banking centre with almost no rules.

Morocco in the early 20th century was under French and Spanish control as protectorates, with its Sultan keeping a formal position. France and Spain both wanted Tangier, and Britain wanted it neutral to protect its position in the strait. They settled this by a convention signed in Paris on 18 December 1923. The zone began on 1 June 1925, with no military presence. In formal terms it still belonged to the Sultan of Morocco.

Government was shared in a careful arrangement. A Committee of Control, made up of the consuls of Belgium, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain, could veto laws, with its chair rotating each year. An appointed International Legislative Assembly made laws. An Administrator held executive power. These were all French until 1940, and later Portuguese, Dutch and Belgian. A representative of the Sultan, the Mendoub, had authority over the Muslim and Jewish communities, who were the majority. A Mixed Court, with judges appointed by Belgium, Britain, Spain, France and Italy, replaced the separate courts each foreign power had run. Italy joined on equal terms in 1928.

The convention made it a tax haven, with no tariffs on goods or gold, no exchange controls and no income or revenue taxes. At first this hurt, because the Spanish authorities around it discouraged trade, and Tangier's share of Morocco's imports fell from 19 percent in 1906 to 4 percent in 1929. Spanish troops occupied the city on 14 June 1940, during the Second World War, and Spain held it until October 1945, when the international system was restored.

After the war, business took off. Tangier had 85 banks in 1950, up from 15 in 1939. There was effectively no bank licensing, supervision or accounting duty, and in some cases a bank's own senior managers did not know who owned it. One author described the place as perfecting the art of not governing, through rival powers cancelling each other out. It was also known for tolerance and drew writers and gay men from Western countries, many of whom could live openly there. By 1956 its population was around 40,000 Muslims, 31,000 Christians and 15,000 Jews.

After France and Spain ended their rule over Morocco in 1956, a protocol signed in Tangier on 29 October 1956 returned the zone to full Moroccan sovereignty, and its buildings became local government offices and courts. The case shows what a real international territory needed, namely a treaty among powerful states, and an underlying sovereign in the background. Its freedom from tax and regulation came from those states' agreement, and it ended once the local state regained its independence.

abkhazia.mechanism: Holding land and running a government can make a territory independent in practice. It stays outside the United Nations without wider recognition from other states, and small states can withdraw recognition later.
abkhazia.story:
