Abkhazia is a territory of about 8,665 square kilometres on the Black Sea coast, in the north-west of Georgia and bordering Russia. Georgia is a country in the Caucasus Mountains that became independent when the Soviet Union broke up. Abkhazia governs itself from the city of Sukhumi, with its own president and laws, but most of the world treats it as part of Georgia. It is one of the clearest modern examples of a place that works like a state and is not accepted as one.

The conflict came with the Soviet collapse. In July 1992 Abkhazia's leaders declared effective independence, and that August Georgia's National Guard entered, starting a war. Abkhaz forces took Sukhumi in September 1993. Up to 250,000 ethnic Georgians were driven out and about 5,000 killed, and summits of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), a body of European and other states, recognised this as ethnic cleansing. A ceasefire followed in 1994, and in October 1999 Abkhazia passed a formal act of independence. 

For years it survived in isolation, under economic sanctions imposed in 1996 by the group of former Soviet republics. In March 2008 Russia announced it would no longer take part in them. During the Russo-Georgian War of August 2008 about 9,000 Russian soldiers entered, and on 26 August Russia recognised Abkhazia's independence. Georgia calls it a Russian-occupied territory.

Daily life shows how much depends on one patron. Russia supplies about half of its budget. The Russian rouble is the currency in practice, and a 2014 agreement ties its economy and customs to Russia. Most residents hold Russian passports, because Abkhazian ones cannot be used for international travel. A person who wants to go abroad therefore travels as a Russian. Tourism is the key industry, with almost a million visitors in 2007 by the authorities' count, mainly from Russia, and it exports wine, tangerines and hazelnuts. Its electricity comes largely from the Inguri dam, on the river between Abkhazia and the rest of Georgia, which both sides run jointly. In the first half of 2012 Russia made up 64 percent of its trade and Turkey 18 percent. About 244,000 people lived there in 2025.

Recognition has been a small and unstable matter. Four UN members recognise it (Russia, Syria, Nicaragua and Venezuela), along with South Ossetia and Transnistria, two other unrecognised states. Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Nauru recognised it and later withdrew. After Assad fell in Syria in December 2024, the Georgian fact-checker Myth Detector found no official withdrawal by Syria as of July 2025. It is not a UN member.

The case shows the difference between holding land and being accepted as a country. Abkhazia has held its land for three decades. Without wider recognition, its people's passports, banks and trade all pass through Russia.

biafra-1967.mechanism: Recognition by other states does not protect a breakaway state that cannot hold its land. Five states recognised Biafra, and it still ended when it lost the war against Nigeria.
biafra-1967.story:
Biafra was a breakaway republic in south-eastern Nigeria, in West Africa, that existed from 1967 to 1970. It covered Nigeria's former Eastern Region and had about 13.5 million people, mainly Igbo with sizeable Ijaw, Efik, Ibibio and other populations. 

Nigeria became independent from Britain in 1960, inside borders that did not follow earlier ethnic or religious lines. The country was split largely along ethnic lines, with a Hausa and Fulani majority in the north, Yoruba in the west and Igbo in the east. Riots against Igbo people had broken out in 1945 in Jos and 1953 in Kano. Disputed elections in 1964 were followed by military coups and a 1966 pogrom against Igbo people in the north. On 30 May 1967 the Eastern Region's governor, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, declared independence. Nigeria's military moved to retake the territory, which started the Nigerian Civil War.

Biafra set up a government and issued its own pound. Five states recognised it officially, Gabon, Haiti, Côte d'Ivoire, Tanzania and Zambia. France, Portugal, Israel, South Africa and Rhodesia treated it as a state in practice and gave covert military support. None of that lifted the Nigerian government's total blockade of the region. Around two million Biafran civilians are estimated to have died in nearly three years of war, and Biafra's surrender came amid starvation caused by the blockade.

Ojukwu fled to Côte d'Ivoire, Vice President Philip Effiong took over and arranged the surrender, and the territory rejoined Nigeria on 15 January 1970. Nigeria's stated motto was no victor, no vanquished. Even so, some Igbo who returned could not get their property back, a loss later fixed in law by the Abandoned Properties Act of 1979. The region remains part of Nigeria, and Igbo nationalism has grown more militant since the 1990s.

For anyone studying how states come to exist, the lesson concerns the limit of recognition. International recognition was real here, by five governments, and it counted for little against a stronger army and a blockade. Recognition did not break the blockade or hold the frontier.

bougainville-2019.mechanism: A peace agreement can promise a vote without promising the outcome. Bougainville's agreement left the final decision with the parliament of the state it wants to leave.

add_sources.t: PNG's parliament Bougainville vote still many months away, Asia Pacific Report

bougainville-2019.story:
Bougainville is an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the South Pacific, made up mainly of a large island east of the main country and north of the Solomon Islands. It voted for independence in 2019 and is still waiting for it. The case shows how a peace deal can promise a vote without promising what follows.

Talk of leaving is old. In 1968 Bougainville's members in the territorial assembly proposed a vote on staying with Papua New Guinea, joining the Solomon Islands or going independent, and no vote was held. Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia in 1975, and Bougainville was made a province in 1976. In 1988 tension turned into civil war between the Bougainville Revolutionary Army and government forces, and one key issue was the Panguna copper mine, which closed in 1989. The war ended with a ceasefire in 1998 and the 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement. That agreement created the Autonomous Bougainville Government and required a referendum some 10 to 15 years after that government's first election.

The vote ran from 23 November to 7 December 2019 and offered a choice of greater autonomy or independence. Independence won 176,928 votes to 3,043, or 98.31 percent, with turnout of 87.38 percent, though press and parliamentary reports in 2026 give the share as 97.7 percent. It was not binding. Under the peace agreement Papua New Guinea's national parliament has the final decision, so the people wanting to leave depend on the votes of those they are leaving.

The wait has been long. In July 2021 the two governments agreed that Bougainville would become independent by 2027, subject to that parliament's approval. In July 2026 a forum of Bougainville leaders recommended 1 September 2030 as the target date. The result was finally tabled in parliament on 27 August 2026. Opposition leader James Nomane complained that MPs had only just received the documents. Prime Minister James Marape said the two governments would meet in October to set a date for the vote. Some MPs fear other provinces might follow, a fear the committee chair Allan Marat called uninformed.

Even a yes would not end the matter. Minister Manasseh Makiba said a yes vote would start a transitional phase of self-government under a plan called the Melanesian Framework and would not bring immediate independence. The two governments could not agree on what happens if parliament votes no. The majority required is also disputed. The national government says two-thirds or three-quarters of an absolute majority, the governing coalition has asked for 89 MPs, and the Bougainville government argues for 60 seats. AAP, an Australian news agency, reports that Bougainville's government plans to declare sovereignty by 2030 if parliament delays further. By November 2026 no date for the vote had been reported.

catalonia-2017.mechanism: A region's vote held against a constitutional court's order has no legal effect within the state. Spain's constitution also let the national government take direct control of the region in response.
catalonia-2017.story:
Catalonia is a region of north-eastern Spain, centred on Barcelona, with its own parliament and government. In 2017 it tried to become independent through a referendum that Spain's courts had blocked. It is the best-known recent test of what happens when a wealthy, well-organised region acts against its own country's constitution.

Pro-independence parties had promised a referendum before the 2015 Catalan election. Their coalition won 62 of 135 seats and governed with the support of 10 members from a smaller party. In the earlier parliament the Catalan government had held only a non-binding citizen consultation. The Spanish government called such a vote a breach of the constitution.

On 6 September 2017 the Catalan parliament, under President Carles Puigdemont, approved a referendum law while 52 opposing members boycotted the vote. The next day Spain's Constitutional Court, which rules on whether laws fit the constitution, suspended the law at the request of the Spanish government. The Catalan government went ahead.

The vote took place on 1 October, and National Police and Civil Guard officers used force at polling stations. Yes took 2,044,038 votes, or 90.18 percent, on a turnout of 43.03 percent. The figures are hard to read, because many opponents stayed away. The Catalan government estimated that up to 770,000 votes could not be cast because of the police action, and observers it had invited said the vote fell short of international standards. The court declared the law void on 17 October.

On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence by 70 votes to 10, with 2 blank and 55 opposition members refusing to take part. The same day Spain's Senate voted 214 to 47 to use Article 155 of the constitution, which lets the national government take direct control of a region's powers when it breaches its duties. The Spanish government had begun that process on 21 October. No state recognised the declaration, so the declared republic had no outside support. 

In the 2024 Catalan elections independence parties lost control of the regional government, and an amnesty was passed that year for crimes linked to the referendum. Catalonia remains part of Spain.

The case shows how much the route matters. Scotland held a lawful vote in 2014 because London agreed. Catalonia had a large movement and an existing regional government, and Madrid did not agree, so its vote had no legal effect inside Spain, and other countries left the matter to Spain.

compacts-of-free-association.mechanism: A territory can become a sovereign state while handing defence to a larger state by treaty in return for funding. The arrangement is known as free association.
compacts-of-free-association.story:
The Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau are three independent countries scattered across the western Pacific that have a special treaty relationship with the United States, called free association. It is a clear example of a way of being a country while handing over one of a country's main jobs.

From 1947 they formed part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, a UN arrangement run by the US Navy until 1951 and then by the Department of the Interior. The agreement obliged the United States to help the people move towards self-government or independence. Each group chose to become a sovereign state, meaning a self-governing country in law, while keeping close ties to the United States.

Referendums in 1983 and 1984 came before the treaties, known as compacts. These took effect on 21 October 1986 for the Marshall Islands, 3 November 1986 for Micronesia and 1 October 1994 for Palau, whose agreement was signed in 1986 and took eight more years to come into force.

The bargain has two sides. The United States pays guaranteed financial assistance and gives access to some US services. In return it holds full authority over their defence, and foreign forces cannot enter without US permission. The United States is responsible for protecting them, although it may not declare war for them. There are limits on it too. It may not use nuclear, chemical or biological weapons in Palau, and it may not store them in the other two except in an emergency. Citizens may serve in the US armed forces, and many do. In 2008 Micronesia had a higher rate of enlistment per person than any US state.

The agreements have no end date, though the economic terms are renewed from time to time. The 2003 renewal gave Micronesia and the Marshall Islands US$3.5 billion, and the most recent covers 2024 to 2043 under US Public Law 118-42. All three remain independent and in association with the United States.

For someone interested in how small places can become states, this model shows that sovereignty can be divided. A tiny country with few resources can gain recognition as a state, while another state pays for its needs and defends it. The arrangement depends on a larger power willing to pay for that control.

eritrea-1993.mechanism: Winning a war gave the Eritrean movement control, and a UN-checked vote then gave other states grounds to accept the result. The combination produced a recognised state.
eritrea-1993.story:
Eritrea is a country on the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa that won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, after a long war and a vote observed by the United Nations. It had been an Italian colony from 1890 and came under British administration after the Second World War. In 1950 the UN voted to join it to Ethiopia in a federation with some self-rule, so its status was decided by outsiders at the start.

By 1962 Ethiopia's Emperor Haile Selassie had ended that self-rule and made Eritrea a province, and an armed rebellion followed. It lasted about three decades. The Eritrean People's Liberation Front, the main rebel movement, first proposed a referendum in 1981. The war ended in May 1991, when the Front defeated Ethiopian forces. At that point the Front controlled Eritrea on the ground.

Transitional governments planned the vote, and a UN mission called UNOVER, set up by the General Assembly in December 1992, observed and checked it. Voting ran from 23 to 25 April 1993, with one question, whether Eritrea should become an independent sovereign state. The result was 99.83 percent yes, 1,100,260 votes against 1,822. Reports of turnout range from 93.93 percent to above 98 percent. Independence was declared on 27 April 1993, and Eritrea joined the UN on 28 May.

Several things came together here that are often missing in other breakaways. Eritrea had a colonial history separate from Ethiopia's, the movement held the land, and the vote was checked by the UN. Other countries had little reason to refuse. Winning a war alone rarely brings acceptance, and a vote alone rarely does either. In this case each gave the other weight.

independence-referendum-record.mechanism: A referendum carries real weight when its terms were agreed with the state being left. A Yes vote without that agreement rarely brings recognition from other states.
independence-referendum-record.story:
An independence referendum is a public vote in which residents decide whether their territory should become a separate country. Many people assume a Yes vote settles the matter. The record shows otherwise, and it is useful as a set of base rates for anyone hoping to found a state this way.

Wikipedia's table lists about 123 such votes up to November 2026, starting with Chile in 1817. Counting its outcomes gives 59 votes ending in a No, 31 in a Yes followed by independence and recognition from other states, 16 in a Yes with no independence, and 12 in a Yes where the territory took control on the ground without general recognition. The rest ended in a status linked to another state, a disputed independence or continuing negotiation. So close to half of these votes end with No, and of those that end with Yes, about half bring a recognised state.

The Yes votes that went nowhere are instructive. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Nevis, in the Caribbean, held an unofficial vote in 1977 that its central government ignored, and voted Yes again in 1998 but fell short of the two-thirds majority required. Iraqi Kurdistan voted Yes in 2005 and 2017 without result. Quebec voted No in 1980 and 1995, which shows that a lawful vote can simply go the other way.

The dividing line is usually consent. Votes held on terms agreed with the state being left can be binding and accepted abroad. South Sudan in 2011 and Montenegro in 2006 are examples. Votes held without that state's consent can lead to one-sided declarations of independence and states that only some countries recognise, as in South Ossetia, or to no change at all, as in Catalonia. There is no international rule that a majority in a region must be obeyed. Other governments decide for themselves whether to recognise the outcome, and most prefer to wait for the parent state's agreement.

katanga-1960.mechanism: A mining company's money and a region's revenue can fund a breakaway government for a time. Whether it lasts depends on outside recognition and force, and here UN troops ended it.
katanga-1960.story:
The State of Katanga was a breakaway republic in the mining south of Congo, in central Africa, from 1960 to 1963. Its capital was Élisabethville, now Lubumbashi, and it covered 496,871 square kilometres with about 1.7 million people. It is the classic case of a secession paid for by a mining company and ended by United Nations troops.

Katanga's copper, uranium and tin are the background. Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, founded in 1906, had the exclusive right to mine copper there, and its main shareholders were Belgian and British bodies, with the Belgian state behind one of them. GlobalSecurity reports that in 1960 Katanga supplied 10 percent of the world's copper and 60 percent of its cobalt. The mining wealth drew about 32,000 Belgians.

Congo became independent from Belgium on 30 June 1960. On 11 July, eleven days after independence, Moïse Tshombe, leader of the local CONAKAT party, declared Katanga independent, saying the central government under Patrice Lumumba was dictatorial and leaned towards communism. Support inside the province was not universal, and ethnic conflict broke out in its north.

Money and foreign help kept it going. Union Minière advanced Tshombe 1,250 million Belgian francs, about US$25 million. Katanga issued its own franc. Belgium's military organised and trained its army, the Katanga Gendarmerie. In September 1960 about 1,133 Belgian technicians and 231 Belgian officers and non-commissioned officers were attached to the government, and in early 1961 nearly 500 British, Rhodesian, French and South African irregular fighters arrived. It even had a small air force. Wikipedia says Belgium gave recognition in practice on 16 July 1960, while GlobalSecurity says Belgium never officially recognised it but gave military, economic and technical help. The United States refused, and no other state gave it general recognition.

Lumumba asked the UN for help. On 14 July 1960 the Security Council called on Belgium to withdraw and set up a UN force, and Lumumba and Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld immediately disagreed over whether it could be used to subdue Katanga. Lumumba was overthrown, then kidnapped and murdered inside the breakaway state, and the secession continued. In February 1961 the Security Council authorised force as a last resort to prevent civil war. Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash during peace talks that year.

UN forces launched Operation Grandslam on 28 December 1962 and held Élisabethville within three days, destroying most of Katanga's planes on the ground. Tshombe conceded in January 1963, UN officials entered his last stronghold, Kolwezi, on 21 January, and Katanga rejoined Congo as a province.

The case shows how far money can carry a new state, and where it stops. A company can pay salaries and hire soldiers, but without recognition the territory cannot join the world's institutions, and it can become a target for them.

kosovo-2008.mechanism: The International Court of Justice said in 2010 that declaring independence does not in itself break international law. Membership of the United Nations still depends on the votes of other states.
kosovo-2008.story:
Kosovo is a territory in the Balkans, in south-eastern Europe, that declared independence from Serbia in 2008 and is recognised by more than half of UN members. Its capital is Pristina, and most of its people are ethnic Albanians. It sits at the point where a territory has many of the signs of statehood and still cannot join the UN.

It had been an autonomous province, one with its own local government, within Serbia, which was then part of Yugoslavia. In 1990 its assembly voted to declare independence, and only Albania recognised that. After the Kosovo War, UN Security Council Resolution 1244 placed it under a UN mission from 1999, with a NATO-led force providing security. As control passed to the UN, an estimated 100,000 Serbs and other non-Albanians fled. So for nine years Kosovo was run by an international body, while remaining formally part of Serbia.

The next step was a plan by the UN Special Envoy Martti Ahtisaari, a former president of Finland, for a kind of supervised independence, without using that word. Kosovo would govern itself under EU supervision, with its own flag and constitutional protection for minorities. Albanian negotiators, the European Union and the United States backed it. Serbia and Russia rejected it, and it broke down in late 2007.

On 17 February 2008, 109 of the 120 assembly members adopted a new declaration of independence. Serbia called it illegal and that year persuaded the UN General Assembly, by 77 votes to 6 with 74 abstentions, to ask the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, for an opinion. On 22 July 2010 the court ruled 10 to 4 that the declaration did not violate international law. The ruling is often misread. The court said that general international law has no ban on declaring independence, and it did not say that Kosovo had become a state or that other countries must recognise it. Declaring is allowed. Whether that makes a state remains up to everyone else.

Later talks facilitated by the EU led to a deal between the governments of Serbia and Kosovo, signed in Brussels in 2013. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members, Taiwan, the Cook Islands and Niue, and 8 other UN members have withdrawn recognition. It belongs to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. It is not a UN member, since admission depends on the votes of other states, and Russia rejected the earlier plan for its status.

For a founder, Kosovo is the most hopeful example of a one-sided declaration, and it also shows what that took. There was a war, foreign troops, nine years of UN rule, and the support of the United States and most of the European Union. Even with all that, full membership of the world's states has stayed out of reach.

montenegro-2006.mechanism: When a union's constitution contains an exit clause, a member has a clear legal way to leave. Because Montenegro used it, outside powers accepted the result within days.
montenegro-2006.story:
Montenegro, a small country on the Adriatic coast in south-eastern Europe, left its union with Serbia in 2006 by using a right written into the union's own constitution. It is the cleanest example of secession by the rules, because the exit door had been built in advance.

When Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s, Serbia and Montenegro stayed together. An earlier vote in Montenegro in 1992 had gone against independence. The 2002 Belgrade Agreement reshaped the relationship, and the Constitutional Charter of Serbia and Montenegro was adopted on 4 February 2003. Its Article 60 allowed a member to leave after at least three years, by referendum.

The fight was over the rules for that vote. The Montenegrin government wanted a simple majority to be enough, and the opposition insisted on a higher bar. A disputed rule requiring 55 percent was adopted. A rule like this matters because a narrow win would leave half the country feeling outvoted.

On 21 May 2006 Yes won 55.5 percent on a turnout of 86.49 percent, 230,711 votes against 184,954, clearing the bar by a narrow margin. All five permanent members of the UN Security Council accepted the preliminary result by 23 May, and the United States, China, Russia and the European Union said they would respect it. Parliament formally declared independence on 3 June, which dissolved the union. Serbia declared itself the union's legal successor, meaning it took over its treaties and memberships, so Montenegro had to apply fresh. It joined the UN on 28 June 2006, about five weeks after the vote.

Kosovo and Abkhazia remain outside the UN years after their declarations. The difference lies in the parent state's consent, given in advance in writing. No outside government had any reason to object, since Serbia itself had signed the agreement that allowed the exit.

new-caledonia-kanaky-referendums.mechanism: An agreed series of votes can run its full course and still leave the question open. Because one side boycotted New Caledonia's last vote, it did not accept the result as settling the matter.
new-caledonia-kanaky-referendums.story:
New Caledonia is a French territory in the South Pacific, east of Australia, known as Kanaky to many of its Indigenous Kanak people. Its future has been argued over through three referendums and years of talks, and it shows that an agreed process can run to the end and leave the question open.

The present arrangements came out of conflict. The Matignon Agreements of 1988 and the Nouméa Accord of 1998, signed by France and the main parties on both sides, set a 20-year transition and allowed up to three votes on independence. 

Voters rejected independence by 57 percent in 2018 and 53 percent in 2020, a gap that was narrowing. The third vote was set for 12 December 2021. Kanak leaders asked for a delay after a COVID-19 outbreak that caused 280 deaths, saying mourning rituals could last a year. Opponents replied that the outbreak had declined by mid-November and accused them of using it as an excuse. France went ahead. The vote took place under a Kanak boycott, and No took 96.5 percent on a turnout of 43.87 percent. Independence supporters did not accept it as settling the matter, since they had boycotted it.

The next crisis was over the voter rolls. Riots in May 2024 over plans to open them, which would let more French nationals vote, killed 14 people and caused over €2 billion in damage. The Bougival accord of July 2025 and the Élysée-Oudinot accord of January 2026 proposed a new status. The FLNKS, the main pro-independence alliance, withdrew from Bougival, saying it had been misled, and boycotted the talks. On 2 April 2026 France's National Assembly rejected the constitutional bill without debate, 190 to 107.

Delayed provincial elections on 28 June 2026, held with about 2,400 police and gendarmes deployed, gave pro-independence parties 26 of 54 Congress seats, the pro-France bloc 24 and the party Éveil Océanien 4. In July 2026 Congress elected the pro-France Virginie Ruffenach as president. Its long-term status remains under talks with France, with no date set.

The case shows the limits of a fair-looking procedure. All sides signed up to three votes, and all three were held. A result that one community refuses to accept still leaves the same dispute, and the same people have to go on living together on the same island.

puntland.mechanism: A region can run its own government and suspend ties with the centre while still saying it belongs to the state. Puntland has done this since 2024 without claiming to be a separate country in law.
puntland.story:
Puntland is a self-governing state in north-east Somalia, on the Horn of Africa, with its capital at Garowe. It covers 212,510 square kilometres, with 1,600 kilometres of coast, and its 2016 population estimate was 4,334,633. It runs itself almost like a country and says it is not one.

Somalia's civil war began in 1991, the year its ruler Siad Barre fell, and the central state stopped working. In the north-west, Somaliland declared itself a separate country. In the north-east, local people took a different course. In 1998 politicians, elders, business people and civil groups held a three-month conference in Garowe, and on 1 August they founded Puntland to provide services, security and trade. It was set up as a homeland for the Harti clan group, with the Majeerteen clan as its chief architects. It has a president, a vice-president and a house of representatives, and it adopted its own constitution at a convention in April 2012.

Its people live from livestock, fishing, frankincense, myrrh and gum arabic, and from farming mangoes, bananas and other crops. Goods imported through Berbera in Somaliland sell more cheaply than those coming through Puntland's port of Bosaso. A maritime police force has worked against piracy and illegal fishing and has also repaired wells and clinics. Unlike Somaliland, its neighbour to the west, Puntland has held that it is part of Somalia, and it disputes the Sool, Sanaag and Ayn regions with Somaliland.

The relationship with the centre then broke down. On 31 March 2024, during a dispute over Somalia's constitution, Puntland said it no longer recognised the federal government, would stop taking part in federal institutions, and would exercise the powers of an independent state until a federal constitution is approved in a referendum it takes part in. No foreign government is known to recognise it as a separate state.

Puntland shows a route that many would-be founders overlook. A region can do almost everything a state does when the state above it has collapsed, with no declaration of independence and so no need for recognition. Its legal position stays that of a part of Somalia.

republic-of-new-afrika.mechanism: A provisional government that claims land by declaration, without the agreement of the state that holds it, gains no territory in law. Here the state answered with raids and prosecutions.
republic-of-new-afrika.story:
The Republic of New Afrika is a Black nationalist organisation in the United States that seeks an independent country in the Black Belt of the American South, the band of states with historically large African American populations. It also demands reparations from the US government for slavery and the Jim Crow segregation laws, and a vote of African Americans on their citizenship. 

Its roots lie in the Black radical movements of the 1960s. Queen Mother Moore and others had drafted a provisional government in 1962, and the Revolutionary Action Movement drew up a nation-within-a-nation programme in 1964. After the Detroit and Newark riots of 1967, activists held a Black Power conference. Then the Malcolm X Society, a Detroit group, called a Black Government Conference in Detroit on 31 March 1968, attended by about 500 people.

It adopted a declaration of independence, a constitution and a provisional government. Robert F. Williams, then in exile in Cuba, was chosen as first president, with Gaidi Obadele (Milton Henry) and Betty Shabazz, the widow of Malcolm X, as vice presidents. The group claimed Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina as "subjugated national territory", and announced a capital on a member's farm in Hinds County, Mississippi. It tried to build institutions, including buying land.

The confrontations that followed decided its fate. Shootouts took place at New Bethel Baptist Church in Detroit in 1969, on the group's first anniversary, and in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1971, in which law-enforcement officers were killed and injured. Members were prosecuted and said they acted in self-defence. The organisation declined in the early 1970s, mainly because of government raids and mass arrests that jailed its leaders.

Its ideas lasted longer. Imari Obadele's books and Nkechi Taifa's Reparations Yes (1993) carried the arguments on. Chokwe Lumumba, elected a vice president in 1971, became a lawyer and was mayor of Jackson from 2013 until his death in 2014. The group still lists officers, though its current activity is not known.

In law, the claim gained no land. A declaration by a provisional government does not move five US states out of the United States, and the federal and state governments treated the group's members as citizens subject to ordinary criminal law. One account describes the state's response as repression of a political movement. Officers were killed in these confrontations, and members were tried for it. No court is known to have ruled on the land claim itself.

sahrawi-republic.mechanism: Membership of a regional body and dozens of recognitions from other states can give a government international standing. They have not given this one control of most of the land it claims.
sahrawi-republic.story:
The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a government in exile for Western Sahara, a desert territory on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa, most of which Morocco holds. It has more diplomatic standing than almost any other unrecognised state, and it has little control of the land it claims.

The territory was a Spanish colony from 1884, known as Spanish Sahara. In 1975 Spain left and handed administration to Morocco and Mauritania under the Madrid Accords. The International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, gave an advisory opinion that October on Moroccan and Mauritanian claims to legal ties with the territory, and on how these related to the local people's right to decide their own future. The Polisario Front, a movement seeking an independent state for the Sahrawi people, proclaimed the republic on 27 February 1976 at Bir Lehlou.

War followed. Mauritania withdrew in 1979, and Morocco built a 2,700-kilometre sand wall dividing the territory. The republic claims 266,000 square kilometres and controls about 90,000 east of the wall, a share given as anywhere from a fifth to 30 percent. It calls that the Liberated Territories, and Morocco calls the rest its Southern Provinces. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum, which never took place because the two sides dispute who may vote. Polisario declared the ceasefire over in November 2020.

Daily life is largely in exile. The official capital, Laayoune, is held by Morocco, and the temporary capital is Tifariti. Most day-to-day government runs from the Rabuni refugee camp near Tindouf, in Algeria, where about 173,600 people lived in 2023, with about 40,000 in the held areas as of 2010. So a government works from another country's soil. The Sahrawi peseta exists on paper, and people use Moroccan dirhams, Algerian dinars, Mauritanian ouguiyas and euros.

It is a full member of the African Union, and counts of recognition range from 33 to 46 UN members, and many others have withdrawn or suspended it. The United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in December 2020. On 31 October 2025 the Security Council voted 11 in favour for talks based on Morocco's autonomy plan. Polisario said the resolution does not imply recognition of Moroccan rule and that it will not join talks aimed at legitimising it. In 2026 Mali said it was withdrawing recognition. The UN still lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory, one whose people have not yet governed themselves.

The case is close to the mirror image of Abkhazia or Puntland, which control their land and lack recognition. The Sahrawi government has recognition and a seat in a regional body, and it is short of land. Recognition also proves to be something that can shrink, one government at a time.

scotland-2014.mechanism: When the parent state agrees to a vote, its result is lawful and accepted by both sides. The UK Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that Scotland cannot hold another without that agreement.

add_sources.t: Proposed second Scottish independence referendum, Wikipedia

scotland-2014.story:
Scotland, a nation within the United Kingdom, held a referendum on independence on 18 September 2014 with the agreement of the UK government. Scotland joined England under the Treaty of Union of 1707, and it has had its own parliament with limited powers since 1999. The case is the model of a secession vote carried out by agreement.

The Scottish National Party, which wants independence, won a majority in the Scottish Parliament in 2011 after promising a vote. That raised a legal problem, because the UK's constitutional arrangements are kept for the UK Parliament. The two governments negotiated until October 2012, when they reached the Edinburgh Agreement. It temporarily gave the Scottish Parliament the legal power to hold the referendum. That deal removed the question of legality, which became the central problem in Catalonia in 2017.

Voters were asked "Should Scotland be an independent country?", and the voting age was lowered from 18 to 16 for the occasion. The Scottish Government published a 670-page white paper on how an independent country would work. The main campaigns were Yes Scotland and Better Together, and they argued over what currency Scotland would use, public spending, EU membership and North Sea oil. An exit poll found that keeping the pound was the deciding factor for many No voters, and that dislike of Westminster politics decided many Yes voters.

No won with 2,001,926 votes, or 55.3 percent, against 1,617,989, or 44.7 percent, and turnout of 84.6 percent was the highest for any UK election or referendum since January 1910. Both governments accepted the result.

Then the ground shifted. In the 2016 vote to leave the European Union, 62 percent of Scottish voters chose to remain, and the party called for a repeat vote. The question of whether a vote could be held without London's agreement went to the courts. On 23 November 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament cannot hold one on its own, since the matter is reserved to the UK Parliament. The UK government has refused to transfer the power again, most recently after the Scottish Parliament asked for it in May 2026 and the Scottish Government published a draft bill that August. Scotland remains part of the United Kingdom.

The lesson runs in both directions. Agreement gave Scotland a vote that everyone accepted. It also meant that the right to ask again rests with the government on the other side.

south-ossetia.mechanism: Repeated Yes votes held without the parent state's agreement did not bring wider recognition. Recognition came mainly from Russia, whose troops hold the territory.
south-ossetia.story:
South Ossetia is a breakaway territory of about 3,900 square kilometres in the Caucasus Mountains, between Georgia and Russia, with its capital at Tskhinvali. Most of the world treats it as part of Georgia. About 53,500 people lived there at a 2015 census, mostly Ossetians, a separate ethnic group from Georgians.

Under the Soviet Union it was an autonomous region of Georgia. As the Soviet Union weakened, it proclaimed a republic in 1990, and Georgia abolished its autonomy that December. Georgian troops entered Tskhinvali in January 1991, and in the war that followed, with Russia backing the Ossetians, about 100,000 Ossetians and 23,000 Georgians fled their homes. A referendum on 19 January 1992 approved independence and joining Russia, and it declared independence on 29 May 1992. A second referendum in 2006 reported 99 percent support, and neither vote brought international recognition. Votes held without the parent state's agreement carry little weight abroad.

War broke out with Georgia in August 2008. Russia invaded and took Tskhinvali, and on 26 August Russia recognised South Ossetia. An EU-sponsored inquiry later said open fighting began with a large Georgian military operation. Georgia calls it occupied territory, and Russia keeps a military base there with thousands of troops.

Economically it is tiny and tied to Russia. Less than 10 percent of its land is farmed, with cereals, fruit and vines, along with forestry and cattle. Its output was estimated at US$15 million in a 2002 study, and its authorities put it near $100 million in 2017. Natural gas has come by pipeline from Russia since 2009.

Four UN members recognise it (Russia, Syria, Nicaragua and Venezuela), along with Abkhazia and Transnistria. Tuvalu and Nauru recognised it and later withdrew. A 2022 plan for a referendum on joining Russia was suspended by a new president. Marat Kambolov has been acting president since June 2026.

The case shows a state that exists on a patron's terms. Its recognition, troops and fuel come mainly from one neighbour. Whether it stays separate depends largely on what that neighbour wants.

south-sudan-2011.mechanism: When the parent state agrees in a peace deal to a vote on separation, with the date fixed in advance, the result is likely to be accepted. Sudan had agreed to the vote and accepted the outcome, so South Sudan was quickly admitted to the UN.
south-sudan-2011.story:
South Sudan, in east-central Africa, became an independent country on 9 July 2011 after voting to leave Sudan. Its path shows what a fully negotiated separation looks like after a long war.

The vote came from the 2005 Naivasha Agreement, also called the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, between the central government in Khartoum and the Sudan People's Liberation Army/Movement, the southern rebel movement. It ended the long war and fixed the terms and date of a referendum in advance. A date set in a peace deal gave both sides something to count on.

For the result to count, turnout had to reach 60 percent, and a simple majority would then mean separation. Getting there was slow. The vote first needed a census, which was delayed three times, and voter registration. Both were hard to carry out because of unmapped minefields in the south, up to 5 million nomadic Sudanese, and up to 2 million displaced southerners in camps around Khartoum.

Voting ran from 9 to 15 January 2011. Final results, published on 7 February, showed 98.83 percent for separation on a turnout of 97.58 percent. Ballots were suspended in 10 of 79 counties because turnout there came to more than 100 percent, and the result was still well above the 60 percent turnout needed. The predetermined date of 9 July then took effect, and South Sudan joined the UN on 14 July 2011, five days later.

One matter stayed unresolved. A parallel vote on whether Abyei, a disputed border area, would join the south was postponed over arguments about borders and who could vote, and it has been put off indefinitely.

South Sudan moved from vote to UN seat within about six months, and for the same reason as Montenegro moved fast. The state being left had signed up to the outcome beforehand, so no one else needed to take sides. What the case shows is limited to the legal process. Agreement made the new state's recognition easy. It says nothing about how well the new country would work once it had its seat.

timor-leste-1999-2002.mechanism: An occupation the UN never accepted can end when the occupying state agrees to a vote. In this case the UN then ran the territory itself until it could become independent.
timor-leste-1999-2002.story:
Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is a country on the eastern half of the island of Timor in South-East Asia that became independent in 2002 after a UN-run vote ended Indonesian rule. Portugal was its colonial ruler. 

In 1975, as Portugal withdrew from its colonies, the independence party Fretilin declared independence. Indonesia invaded that December and annexed the territory the following year. The UN did not recognise the annexation, so in the UN's eyes the territory was never Indonesian. That mattered a great deal 24 years later. The Dili massacre of 12 November 1991 drew world attention, and in 1996 two East Timorese leaders, Bishop Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta, received the Nobel Peace Prize.

The opening came with a change of leader. B. J. Habibie succeeded President Suharto in March 1998, and on 27 January 1999 he agreed to let voters choose between special autonomy within Indonesia and independence. A 5 May agreement between Indonesia and Portugal set the terms, and a UN mission ran the ballot.

On 30 August 1999, 78.5 percent of voters rejected autonomy, on a turnout of 98.93 percent. Militias favouring Indonesia then carried out mass violence and destruction, and a UN-backed inquiry later held the Indonesian army and militias responsible for widespread killing and forced displacement. On 15 September the UN Security Council approved a multinational force led by Australia, INTERFET, to restore order. Indonesia's assembly repealed its 1978 annexation resolution. Many Indonesians, including the government, call the vote a consultation.

Then the UN did something rare. The UN Transitional Administration in East Timor (UNTAET) governed the territory directly until independence on 20 May 2002. Timor-Leste joined the UN that September.

Several things made success possible here. The UN had never accepted the annexation, the occupying state changed its government, outsiders ran the vote, and foreign troops enforced the result. The killing after the vote also shows what can follow when a ballot takes place without security in place.

blueseed.mechanism: A ship just beyond the 12-mile limit lies outside a state's full control, so work done on board might not need a work visa. The idea was never tested because the ship was never leased.
blueseed.story:
Blueseed was a company in Palo Alto, California, founded on 31 July 2011 by Max Marty, Dario Mutabdzija and Dan Dascalescu. It began as a seasteading venture, meaning an attempt to live and work on the open sea. It planned to house startup founders on a ship anchored 12 nautical miles off the California coast near Silicon Valley.

The problem it set out to solve was immigration law. A foreign entrepreneur who wants to start a company in the United States generally needs a work visa, such as the H-1B, and these are limited. Blueseed's idea was that founders could work on a ship outside US waters and travel to the mainland on easier business or tourist visas to meet investors.

The location was chosen with care. The territorial sea, the belt of water a state fully controls, extends 12 nautical miles from the coast. Just beyond it lies the contiguous zone, where a coastal state has only limited powers to enforce its customs, tax, immigration and health rules. The theory was that the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea would allow the ship to stay there, as long as it did not exploit natural resources and did not appear to be breaking those US laws. It would have flown the flag of an open registry country such as the Marshall Islands or the Bahamas, which would decide the law on board. The company said gambling and prostitution would be banned.

The project received wide press coverage and a promise of investment from Peter Thiel, the technology investor, who did not invest in the seed round, the first stage of funding. It reported US$300,000 in seed funding, some Bitcoin investments and $9 million from an undisclosed investor, and said it would lease a ship. Its launch date moved from the third quarter of 2013 to late 2014, on the assumption that $18 million more would come in. The money did not arrive, and the project went on hold in 2013. The company reportedly resumed in 2020 as a business accelerator, a programme that helps new firms, and dropped the ship.

The legal plan was never tested. It was also not a claim to be outside all law. A flag state's law would apply on board, and residents would still need US visas to come ashore. It offered a place to work, within rules, and it ended for the reason most ventures do, lack of money.

freedom-ship.mechanism: The idea behind Freedom Ship is that a constantly moving vessel escapes tax and property law. That idea remains untested because the ship was never financed, and any ship would still need a flag state, the country whose law applies on board.
freedom-ship.story:
Freedom Ship is a floating city proposed in the late 1990s by the engineer Norman Nixon, meant to be a mobile colony free of the property, local and national laws of any state. It has never been built. The main aim was to save taxes, since the ship would keep moving around the world, and its residents would never stay long in any one country.

The plan was a chain of linked barges 1,800 metres long and 250 metres wide, with 25 floors and homes for about 80,000 people. There would be 50,000 living units, 3,000 commercial units and 10,000 hotel units, plus a hospital, schools, a casino and duty-free shops. For comparison, the largest ship ever built, the Seawise Giant, was about a quarter of that length. It would constantly circle the globe, stopping at ports.

The story since has mostly been about money. The company, Freedom Ship International, estimated the cost at US$6 billion in 1999 and US$11 billion by 2002. A press release in July 2008 explained how hard it was to find reliable funding. In November 2013 the company said the project was being revived at US$10 billion, with construction not yet begun, and in 2016 it was linked to Kanethara Marine in India. By 2026 estimates had reached US$15 billion and then US$20 billion. In June 2026 Euronews reported a redesign by the Florida-based Freedom Cruise Line International, led by Roger Gooch, expected to use nuclear fuel and to be built in Indonesia once funded. No launch date has been given, and no ship has been built.

The legal idea would run into the ordinary rules of the sea. A ship at sea needs a flag state, the country where it is registered and whose law applies on board. In every port it would be under the port country's laws for the time it stayed. Residents would remain citizens of their home countries, and those countries decide for themselves how to tax their citizens. So a moving ship could reduce some taxes for some people, depending on their citizenship, but it would not by itself place them outside every country's law. The idea has not been tested, because it has never been financed.

life-at-sea.mechanism: A contract to live on a ship is an ordinary consumer contract under national law. Buyers' protection depends on the company being able to pay and on courts on land.
life-at-sea.story:
Life at Sea Cruises was a company, with Miray Cruises as its parent, that sold a three-year round-the-world voyage in which passengers would live aboard at prices it said rivalled ordinary living costs. It made no claim of sovereignty, but it shows what buyers risked when they paid a private company for a home at sea before any ship existed.

The voyage was due to leave Istanbul, Turkey, on 1 November 2023. Shortly before that, the date moved to 11 November and the port to Amsterdam, and then to 30 November. On 17 November passengers were told the cruise was off, and after weeks of silence the company admitted it had no ship. Some of the buyers of the 111 cabins sold were already in Istanbul, and others said they had sold or let their homes and given away their possessions. Most had spent tens of thousands of dollars, and some cruises cost up to hundreds of thousands.

The company promised repayment in monthly instalments from mid-December to late February, and offered to pay for flights home and hotels until 1 December. By January 2024 only four passengers had received refunds, and 78 customers asked the US attorney in southern Florida, the federal prosecutor there, to open a criminal investigation over about $16 million in deposits. How that request ended is not known.

A similar venture later failed in a different way. Villa Vie Residences, based in Florida, launched its ship Odyssey on a continuous world voyage in October 2024, selling cabins for several hundred thousand dollars, with monthly fees on top. On about 27 October 2026 it halted operations and sent more than 200 residents, most of them American, ashore at Sihanoukville, Cambodia. Its chief executive, Mikael Petterson, blamed fuel prices, which he said rose from about $700 a ton to $2,000 or $3,000 after the war with Iran began. He said the company would file for Chapter 11, the US bankruptcy process. A resident disputed the company's claim that it was paying for lodging.

These cases show what living at sea means in law. A cabin bought on a ship is a contract with a company, and the buyer gets the rights in that contract. When a company fails, buyers join a queue of creditors under the law of whichever country has authority over it. They do not own a piece of land, and they have no state of their own to turn to, only the courts and prosecutors of the places where the company operates.

ms-satoshi.mechanism: A ship's legal status at sea depends in practice on private insurers. Without liability insurance a ship cannot keep a crew, a class rating or a flag, and so has no lawful standing.
ms-satoshi.story:
MS Satoshi was a 1991 cruise ship that the company Ocean Builders, led by chief executive Grant Romundt, bought in 2020 to turn into a floating community in the Gulf of Panama. The ship had sailed for P&O as the Pacific Dawn and earlier as the Regal Princess. The plan was aimed partly at cryptocurrency companies. Ocean Builders was also developing floating off-grid homes called seapods.

The company announced the plan in early October 2020, and took delivery on 5 November. The ship would be anchored full-time, with cabins auctioned as homes for entrepreneurs, expats, digital nomads and cryptocurrency companies, with vacation rentals and businesses running restaurants and entertainment on board. The first residents were expected as early as January 2021. The ship sailed from Gibraltar, where it had been overhauled, towards Panama.

No government or navy acted against the project. Romundt told investors the project could not go on, because no protection and indemnity insurer would cover it. That is the liability cover a ship's owners need against claims at sea. The chain of consequences is what makes the case useful. Without insurance there could be no crew. Without crew the ship would lose its class rating, the safety certificate from a ship inspection body, and its flag, the national registration a ship needs. Without those there could be no lawful businesses on board.

He wrote that assuming a stationary residential ship would be easy to insure had been incorrect, and he blamed "archaic big insurance companies". The ship was sold for scrap on 18 December 2020 and was to go on to India. Trade press later reported that it was arrested in Panama, meaning held by court order, then released and sold to a new cruise startup in 2021.

Founders tend to prepare for arguments about sovereignty. This case shows that the practical limit on life at sea may be private institutions, with no state having to act. No government had challenged the project before it ended.

ms-the-world.mechanism: People can live permanently at sea without claiming any country of their own by using an ordinary flag registration. The flag state, the country where the ship is registered, supplies the law on board.
ms-the-world.story:
MS The World is a private ship run like a block of flats, with 165 residences (106 apartments, 19 studio apartments and 40 studios) owned by the people who live on it. It is 196 metres long, with 12 decks. It is a working example of permanent life at sea, and it claims no special legal status.

It was the idea of Knut Kloster, from a family long in the shipping business, and it was first announced as The World of ResidenSea. It was ordered in 2000, with the hull built in Sweden and finished in Norway, completed on 20 February 2002, and bought by its residents in October 2003.

Its port of registry is Nassau in the Bahamas, which means the ship flies the Bahamian flag and Bahamian law applies on board at sea. In port, the law of that country also applies. ROW Management runs it from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and it handles operations and hires the staff. Residents come from many countries. Some live on board full-time, while others visit from time to time. They elect a board that advises the management company on the route and finances, much as owners in a block of flats elect a committee. On average it carries 150 to 200 residents and guests, with a crew of about 280. The route includes remote places. On 28 January 2017, with 63 residents aboard, it set a record as the southernmost ship, later surpassed.

It emptied in March 2020 because of COVID-19 and returned to service in July 2021.

It makes no claim to statehood. Residents remain citizens of their own countries. Compare it with Freedom Ship, which aimed to carry 80,000 people free of national law and was never built, or MS Satoshi, which could not get insurance. The World was built by shipping professionals as an ordinary registered ship, with ordinary crew, insurance and a flag state. On this evidence the most workable form of permanent life at sea is a conventional ship, and it creates no new legal territory for those on board.
